Abstract




Differential Equations for Massive Correlators

Abstract

We uncover a combinatorial structure governing the differential equations satisfied by wavefunction coefficients of scalar fields with generic masses in de Sitter space. Using an integral representation of the massive mode functions, we express the Feynman integrals underlying cosmological correlators as twisted integrals of rational functions. In this formulation, the integrals belong to a finite set of master integrals obeying a first-order system of differential equations, which can be derived efficiently in the time-integral representation. We show that these equations admit a simple graphical description in terms of graph tubings, which encode the couplings among basis functions and the evolution of singularities. This structure provides an efficient algorithm to derive the differential equations, and a boundary-centric perspective on massive cosmological correlators in which their analytic structure emerges from underlying combinatorial data. As an illustration, we solve the system in the limits of small and large masses.

1
Introduction

An important feature of cosmology is that space itself is dynamical and evolves in time.
This complicates the quantum-mechanical sum over all possible times that processes can occur, because particle interactions typically also change in time.
Consequently, even tree-level computations of cosmological correlators involve nontrivial time integrals over propagators and interaction vertices
[
12
,
10
,
16
]
. In addition, in the curved spacetimes relevant for cosmology, the free-field mode functions are generically complicated special functions. Combined, these features make it difficult to evaluate the Feynman integrals underlying cosmological correlation functions in closed form.

Despite these challenges, there are remarkable structures underlying cosmological observables that make their study tractable.
One way to glimpse these features is to consider how cosmological correlations change as we change the parameters they depend on.
For example, if we smoothly vary the kinematics,
we expect observables to change continuously and therefore to satisfy differential equations that describe how their strength changes. In
[
2
]
, these differential equations were studied in a simplified setting involving conformally coupled scalars with polynomial interactions in a power-law cosmology
[
5
]
. The integrals of interest are then generalized Euler integrals, which have close connections to the mathematics of twisted cohomology and hyperplane arrangements, as well as a beautiful geometric interpretation related to cosmological polytopes
[
5
]
. A consequence of these mathematical connections is that these cosmological integrals belong to a finite-dimensional basis of master integrals
I_{a}
, which satisfy differential equations of the form

{\rm d}I_{a}=A_{ab}\,I_{b}\,,

(1.1)

where
{\rm d}
is a differential with respect to kinematic variables, and
A_{ab}
is a matrix of one-forms that encodes the singularities of the differential system.
Remarkably, these differential equations have a simple combinatorial description, called
kinematic flow

[
2
,
3
,
8
]
, which generates the connection matrix
A_{ab}
. (Additional features have been studied in
[
25
,
26
,
31
,
41
,
35
,
19
,
46
,
33
]
.) Aside from providing an efficient algorithm to derive these differential equations, this structure reveals an intriguing boundary-centric perspective on cosmological correlations, where they arise from purely combinatorial origins
[
3
]
.

It is natural to wonder whether the structures seen in the conformally coupled case are merely artifacts of the toy nature of the setup, or whether they can be abstracted to more general (and phenomenologically relevant) settings involving massive particles
[
23
,
11
,
48
,
6
,
44
,
4
,
7
,
52
,
54
,
17
,
50
,
43
]
. In this paper, we address this question by finding similar combinatorial structures in the differential equations satisfied by correlators and wavefunction coefficients of scalar fields with arbitrary masses in exact de Sitter space.
1
1

1

Wavefunctions and correlation functions in de Sitter space satisfy the same differential equations; they differ only in the boundary conditions used to solve them. As a result, the methods developed here apply equally to both cases. The same tools can also be used to compute boundary correlators in Euclidean AdS.

Related aspects of this problem have also been considered recently in
[
15
,
22
,
21
,
45
,
34
,
47
,
55
,
51
,
56
,
13
]
.

The most obvious complication is that the mode functions of
massive fields in de Sitter space are Hankel functions. This leads to a richer structure of integrands, compared to the conformally coupled case.
One way to deal with this is to express the Hankel functions as integrals over auxiliary parameters, which makes it possible to cast the associated wavefunction coefficients as integrals over rational functions times a twist factor that depends on the mass parameter
[
34
]
.
An interesting feature of this perspective is that the wavefunction for an arbitrary process involving generic masses can be written in terms of a
universal integrand
, which itself has a combinatorial definition. This guarantees that the wavefunction of interest still lies in a finite-dimensional space of twisted integrals which satisfies a system of differential equations.

While the twisted-integral representation guarantees the existence of a system of differential equations, in order to actually derive these equations it is simplest to go back to the time-integral representation.
This representation assembles the wavefunction from a natural set of time-ordered pieces.
In addition, it is convenient to enlarge the function basis by essentially including a second copy of all basis functions where we replace the mode functions with their first derivatives
[
22
,
21
]
. We then write all basis elements in terms of the following functions

h_{k}^{\pm}(\eta)\propto(-k\eta)^{\nu}H_{\nu}^{(2)}(-k\eta)\mp i\frac{\partial}{\partial k\eta}\Big[(-k\eta)^{\nu}H_{\nu}^{(2)}(-k\eta)\Big]\,,

(1.2)

which are linear combinations of the de Sitter mode function and its first derivative. The benefit of these combinations is that they satisfy
first-order
differential equations.
Fundamentally, this underlies the existence of a first-order system in the time-integral representation. As an example, we can write the (time-ordered) wavefunction coefficient for a single massive exchange as a sum of functions of the form

\displaystyle\psi^{({\color[rgb]{0.8398,0.1523,0.1563}{\pm}}{\color[rgb]{0.1211,0.4648,0.707}{\pm}})}

(1.3)

\displaystyle=\int{\rm d}\eta_{1}{\rm d}\eta_{2}\,\frac{e^{iX_{1}\eta_{1}}e^{iX_{2}\eta_{2}}}{(-\eta_{1})^{1+\alpha_{1}+\xi}(-\eta_{2})^{1+\alpha_{2}+\xi}}\Big[\bar{h}^{{\color[rgb]{0.8398,0.1523,0.1563}{\pm}}}_{Y}(\eta_{1})h^{{\color[rgb]{0.1211,0.4648,0.707}{\pm}}}_{Y}(\eta_{2})\,\theta_{12}+h^{{\color[rgb]{0.8398,0.1523,0.1563}{\pm}}}_{Y}(\eta_{1})\bar{h}^{{\color[rgb]{0.1211,0.4648,0.707}{\pm}}}_{Y}(\eta_{2})\,\theta_{21}\Big]\,,

where
\theta_{ij}\equiv\theta(\eta_{i}-\eta_{j})

are the external energies entering each vertex and

\alpha_{1}
and
\alpha_{2}

\xi\equiv\nu-\tfrac{1}{2}
characterizes the deviation of the mass from the conformally coupled value. Differentials of these basis functions have an elegant interpretation in terms of collapsing the propagators of the underlying Feynman diagram. For example, the differential of the functions in (

) is

\displaystyle{\rm d}\psi^{({\color[rgb]{0.8398,0.1523,0.1563}{\pm}}{\color[rgb]{0.1211,0.4648,0.707}{\pm}})}

\displaystyle=\Big[\alpha_{1}\,{\rm d}\log(X_{1}\,{\color[rgb]{0.8398,0.1523,0.1563}{\pm}}\,Y)+\alpha_{2}\,{\rm d}\log(X_{2}\,{\color[rgb]{0.1211,0.4648,0.707}{\pm}}\,Y)\Big]\,\psi^{({\color[rgb]{0.8398,0.1523,0.1563}{\pm}}{\color[rgb]{0.1211,0.4648,0.707}{\pm}})}-\frac{{\color[rgb]{0.8398,0.1523,0.1563}{\pm}}1{\color[rgb]{0.1211,0.4648,0.707}{\mp}}1}{2}\hskip 1.0pt{\rm d}\log\left(\frac{X_{1}\,{\color[rgb]{0.8398,0.1523,0.1563}{\pm}}\,Y}{X_{2}\,{\color[rgb]{0.1211,0.4648,0.707}{\pm}}\,Y}\right)J^{(c)}

(1.4)

\displaystyle+\xi\bigg[{\rm d}\log\left(\frac{X_{1}\,{\color[rgb]{0.8398,0.1523,0.1563}{\pm}}\,Y}{Y}\right)\,\psi^{({\color[rgb]{0.8398,0.1523,0.1563}{\mp}}{\color[rgb]{0.1211,0.4648,0.707}{\pm}})}+{\rm d}\log\left(\frac{X_{2}\,{\color[rgb]{0.1211,0.4648,0.707}{\pm}}\,Y}{Y}\right)\psi^{({\color[rgb]{0.8398,0.1523,0.1563}{\pm}}{\color[rgb]{0.1211,0.4648,0.707}{\mp}})}\bigg]\,,

where
{\rm d}\equiv\sum_{i}{\rm d}X_{i}\partial_{X_{i}}+{\rm d}Y\partial_{Y}
. Notice that the source functions appearing on the right-hand side of (
1.4
) are related to the original function by sign flips of the
\pm
indices, along with the function

J^{(c)}
that arises from collapsing the internal propagator to a contact diagram. The dlog-forms (“letters”) multiplying these source functions also display apparent structure.
A similar pattern persists for generic diagrams with arbitrary masses, including loop integrands.

The differential equations satisfied by the wavefunction coefficients clearly have some combinatorial underpinnings.
In
[
2
,
8
]
, the structures underlying similar differential equations were elucidated by representing the basis functions and possible singularities by graph tubings.
Two simple rules then governed how the functions are coupled and how the singularities “evolve” when taking derivatives with respect to the kinematic variables.
We will show that a similar graphical representation also reveals the underlying structure of the differential equations in the massive case.

\lxSVG@closescope {{
{}{}{}{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces}{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces}}}{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces}{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces}\hss}\lxSVG@discardpath\lxSVG@closescope \hss}}\lxSVG@closescope\endpgfpicture}}}\Big)\psi_{\includegraphics[scale]{Figures/Tubings/Functions/psimm.pdf}}\Big]\,,

where each colored tube represents a letter related to the total energy enclosed by the tube.
This pictorial representation makes clear that the differential equations have a dynamical interpretation in the space of tubings.
The first line in (
1.5
) is the same as for conformally coupled fields, while the second line (proportional to
\xi
) is a novelty of massive fields. We see that massive propagators lead to additional basis functions, and we expand the meaning of the graph tubings to capture these functions. In the conformally coupled case, tubes can only “grow” by the merger of adjacent tubes, corresponding to the collapse of the internal propagator (like in the function
J_{\includegraphics[scale]{Figures/Tubings/Functions/psic.pdf}}
in the above example). Tubes enclosing a massive propagator, on the other hand, can also “shrink” to create an exposed cross or grow to produce overlapping tubes. In the above examples, this creates the new functions
\psi_{\includegraphics[scale]{Figures/Tubings/Functions/psipp.pdf}}
and
\psi_{\includegraphics[scale]{Figures/Tubings/Functions/psimm.pdf}}
, respectively. We formulate an additional kinematic flow rule that accounts for this new phenomenon.

The first-order system produced by this massive flow provides some interesting new perspectives on familiar phenomena. Broadly in this formalism, physical solutions are selected by specifying boundary data for the system, which further reinforces the perspective of cosmological observables as arising from a flow through kinematic space. Beyond this, the organization of the equations makes taking parametric mass limits particularly transparent.
In order to illustrate this, we solve the differential equations for a single massive exchange between conformal scalars both in the limit where the mass is taken to infinity, and where it approaches its conformally coupled value.
The large-mass limit is closely connected to the effective field theory expansion, which arises in an intriguing way from the first-order system. In the infinite-mass limit, the equations become algebraic, and so the perturbative expansion about this point can be solved recursively. This expansion can be formally re-summed to match the EFT expansion of
[
4
]
.
In the conformally coupled limit, the observables simplify to polylogarithmic functions, and the differential equations encode the symbol (sequence of branch points) of these functions
[
2
]
. As we expand about this limit, the perturbative corrections in mass can also be expressed in terms of polylogarithmic functions
[
34
]
, though with a more intricate structure.

It is rather interesting that the differential equations for massive fields display a similar richness to the conformally coupled case. This suggests that the interesting structures discovered in the conformal case are more far-reaching than has been previously appreciated.
In addition, the fact that all masses can be treated uniformly provides a universal parameterization of processes relevant for phenomenology, but encoded in a language that is more amenable to the formal study of their fundamental properties.

Outline

The paper is organized as follows. In Section
2
, we introduce the Feynman integrals that compute wavefunction coefficients involving massive fields, and explain that they are part of a finite-dimensional vector space of master integrals. In Section
3
, we choose a convenient basis and derive the associated differential equations for several representative examples, uncovering simple and universal patterns in the connection matrix that governs the couplings among the basis functions. In Section
4
, we show that these patterns are naturally explained by a straightforward generalization of the kinematic flow rules. In Section
5
, we solve the differential equations in the limits of small and large masses, illustrating the method with the example of the single massive exchange. Finally, we summarize our conclusions in Section
6
.

Three appendices contain supplemental material. In Appendix
A
, we describe a mapping between massive fields in de Sitter space and massless fields in a power-law cosmology, which allows the results for massive fields to be translated directly to the massless setting by appropriately mapping parameters. In Appendix
B
, we show how the massive integrals can be expressed as twisted integrals of rational functions, with twists given by the deviation from the conformally coupled mass. We further discuss the geometry and combinatorics underlying the universal integrand. Finally, in Appendix
C
, we
demonstrate that the kinematic flow algorithm also applies to loop integrands, in a way that is more uniform than the conformal case.

2
Massive Integrals

We begin by introducing the Feynman integrals that appear in the computation of cosmological correlators. In theories containing massive fields, the integrands involve products of Hankel functions, which makes these integrals difficult to evaluate directly. By employing an integral representation of the Hankel functions, we rewrite these expressions as twisted integrals of rational functions. This reformulation allows us to show that the relevant integrals belong to a finite-dimensional vector space spanned by a set of master integrals. In Section
3
, we derive differential equations satisfied by these integrals.

2.1
Massive Fields in de Sitter

We will consider minimally coupled massive scalar fields in a rigid
(d+1)
-dimensional de Sitter spacetime, with polynomial interactions

S=\int{\rm{d}}^{d+1}x\,\sqrt{-g}\left[-\frac{1}{2}(\partial\phi)^{2}-\frac{1}{2}m^{2}\phi^{2}-\sum_{p=3}^{\infty}\frac{\lambda_{p}}{p!}\phi^{p}\right].

(2.1)

The spacetime metric is of the Robertson–Walker form
{{\rm{d}}s}^{2}=a^{2}(\eta)(-{\rm{d}}\eta^{2}+{\rm{d}}{\bf{x}}^{2})
, with scale factor

a(\eta)=\frac{1}{H(-\eta)}\,,

(2.2)

where
\eta\in(-\infty,0)
is conformal time and
H
is the Hubble constant. We are interested in computing correlation functions at the future boundary, which we denote by
\eta_{*}=0
.
The initial conditions are imposed at
\eta\to-\infty
, when all modes are deep inside the horizon.

A free massive field satisfies the Euler–Lagrange equation derived from the quadratic part of the action (
2.1
). In momentum space, this is given by

\left[\frac{\partial^{2}}{\partial\eta^{2}}-\frac{(d-1)}{\eta}\frac{\partial}{\partial\eta}+\left(k^{2}+\frac{m^{2}}{H^{2}\eta^{2}}\right)\right]\phi_{\bf{k}}(\eta)=0\,.

(2.3)

This differential equation can be cast into the form of Bessel’s equation, whose solution can be written as

\phi_{\bf{k}}(\eta)=f_{k}(\eta)\hskip 1.0pt\alpha_{{\bf{k}}}\,,

(2.4)

where
\alpha_{{\bf{k}}}
are constants that depend on initial conditions, and
f_{k}(\eta)
is a mode function.
2
2

2

The mode function is normalized so that its Wronskian is
f^{*}\partial_{\eta}f-f\partial_{\eta}f^{*}=i(-H\eta)^{d-1}
. This ensures that the canonically quantized field has the correct commutation relations when
\alpha_{\textbf{k}}
is promoted to an annihilation operator.

Assuming Bunch–Davies initial conditions, the mode function takes the following explicit form

f_{k}(\eta)=\frac{\sqrt{\pi H^{d-1}}}{2}e^{-i\frac{\pi\nu}{2}}(-\eta)^{d/2}H^{(2)}_{\nu}(-k\eta)\,,

(2.5)

where
H^{(2)}_{\nu}
is the Hankel function of the second kind, with

\nu\equiv\sqrt{\frac{d^{2}}{4}-\frac{m^{2}}{H^{2}}}\,.

(2.6)

Depending on the mass value, the parameter
\nu
is either purely real or purely imaginary. Unitary representations correspond to the range
-d/2<\nu<d/2
(
complementary series
) and
\nu=i\mu
, with
\mu\in{\mathbb{R}}
(
principal series
). Since the system is invariant under the shadow symmetry
\nu\leftrightarrow-\nu
, it is convenient to adopt the convention
\mathop{\mathrm{Re}}\nu\geq 0
or
\mathop{\mathrm{Im}}\nu\geq 0
.
The conformally coupled mass
m^{2}/H^{2}=(d^{2}-1)/4
corresponds to
\nu=\tfrac{1}{2}
, and it will be useful to define the deviation away from this value as
\xi\equiv\nu-\tfrac{1}{2}
.

2.2
Wavefunction Coefficients

Cosmological data is encoded in correlation functions. We are interested in correlation functions of the scalar field
\phi(\eta,{\bf{x}})
at the late-time boundary
\eta_{*}=0
.
These correlation functions can be calculated using the Born rule:

\langle\varphi({\bf{x}}_{1})\cdots\varphi({\bf{x}}_{n})\rangle=\int\mathcal{D}\varphi\;\varphi({\bf{x}}_{1})\cdots\varphi({\bf{x}}_{n})\left|\Psi\left[\varphi\right]\right|^{2}\,,

(2.7)

where
\varphi({\bf{x}})\equiv\phi(\eta_{*},{\bf{x}})
is the boundary value of the field. In other words, by summing over all possible profiles of
n
insertions of fields with the weight given by the square of the wavefunction,
|\Psi[\varphi]|^{2}
, one obtains the
n
-point correlation function. For small fluctuations, the wavefunction can be expanded as

\Psi[\varphi]=\exp\left[-\sum_{n=2}^{\infty}\frac{1}{n!}\int\frac{{\rm d}^{d}k_{1}}{(2\pi)^{d}}\cdots\frac{{\rm d}^{d}k_{n}}{(2\pi)^{d}}\,(2\pi)^{d}\delta(\textbf{k}_{1}+\dots+\textbf{k}_{n})\,\psi_{n}(\underline{\textbf{k}})\,\varphi_{\textbf{k}_{1}}\cdots\varphi_{\textbf{k}_{n}}\right],

(2.8)

where
\psi_{n}
are the
wavefunction coefficients
. These wavefunction coefficients can be expressed as a sum over Feynman diagrams, and it is these diagrams that we aim to compute.

In momentum space, the
n
-point wavefunction coefficients depend on

n
Euclidean momentum vectors,
\underline{{\bf{k}}}=\{{\bf{k}}_{1},\cdots\hskip-1.0pt,{\bf{k}}_{n}\}
.
We denote their magnitudes by

k_{a}=|{\bf{k}}_{a}|
, and refer to them as “energies” in a small abuse of terminology.
Spatial translation invariance of the background spacetime implies momentum conservation at each vertex, so that the momenta form a closed polygon. The shape of this polygon is determined by the lengths of its edges and diagonals, so
wavefunction coefficients can be expressed in terms of external and internal energies.

Feynman rules

The contributions to the wavefunction are computed using the following
Feynman rules
:

•

External lines:
Every external line corresponds to a bulk-to-boundary propagator:

\displaystyle\raisebox{-10.0pt}{
\hbox to24.76pt{\vbox to23.12pt{\pgfpicture\makeatletter\hbox{\hskip 12.38092pt\lower-2.20715pt\hbox to0.0pt{\lxSVG@begingroup@{_scopebegin} \lxSVG@begingroup@{stroke} \lxSVG@begingroup@{fill} \lxSVG@setlinewidth{\the\pgflinewidth}\lxSVG@begingroup@{stroke-width} \lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\nullfont\hbox to0.0pt{\lxSVG@begingroup@{_scopebegin} {{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces}}\lxSVG@setlinewidth{\the\pgflinewidth}\lxSVG@begingroup@{stroke-width} \lx@inpgf@ignorespaces
{}{{}}{}
{}{}\lxSVG@begingroup@{_scopebegin} \lxSVG@setlinewidth{\the\pgflinewidth}\lxSVG@begingroup@{stroke-width} \lx@inpgf@ignorespaces{}\lxSVG@stroke\lxSVG@drawpath@unclipped{M 0 0 L 0 27.56}{fill:none} \lx@inpgf@ignorespaces
\lxSVG@closescope {}{{}}{}
{}{}\lxSVG@begingroup@{_scopebegin} \color[rgb]{0.75,0.75,0.75}\lxSVG@setlinewidth{\the\pgflinewidth}\lxSVG@begingroup@{stroke-width} \lx@inpgf@ignorespaces{}\lxSVG@stroke\lxSVG@drawpath@unclipped{M -15.75 27.56 L 15.75 27.56}{fill:none} \lx@inpgf@ignorespaces
\lxSVG@closescope {}{{}}{}{{{}}{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces}{}{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces}{}{}{}{}{}}\lxSVG@begingroup@{_scopebegin} \lxSVG@begingroup@{fill} {}\lxSVG@fillstroke\lxSVG@drawpath@unclipped{M 0 0 M 2.36 0 C 2.36 1.3 1.3 2.36 0 2.36 C -1.3 2.36 -2.36 1.3 -2.36 0 C -2.36 -1.3 -1.3 -2.36 0 -2.36 C 1.3 -2.36 2.36 -1.3 2.36 0 Z M 0 0}{} \lx@inpgf@ignorespaces
\lxSVG@closescope
\lxSVG@closescope {\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces}{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces}{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces}\hss}\lxSVG@discardpath\lxSVG@closescope \hss}}\lxSVG@closescope\endpgfpicture}}
}

\displaystyle\equiv

\displaystyle\ K(k,\eta)

\displaystyle=

\displaystyle\frac{f_{k}(\eta)}{f_{k}(\eta_{*})}\,,

(2.9)

where the mode function
f_{k}(\eta)
is a solution to the equation of motion for the field
\phi_{{\bf{k}}}(\eta)
. For Bunch–Davies initial conditions, the mode functions at large
|k\eta|
(i.e. at early times or on small scales) reduce to their Minkowski space counterparts,
f_{k}(\eta)\sim e^{+ik\eta}
.

•

Internal lines:
Every internal line corresponds to a bulk-to-bulk propagator:

\displaystyle\includegraphics[valign,scale]{Figures/Equations/SolidPropagator.pdf}\ \ \ \equiv\ \ G(k,\eta,\eta^{\prime})

\displaystyle=\ \ \ G_{\text{F}}(k,\eta,\eta^{\prime})\ \,-\ \ \,G_{\text{D}}(k,\eta,\eta^{\prime})

(2.10)

\displaystyle=\ \ \includegraphics[valign,scale]{Figures/Equations/CrossedPropagator.pdf}\ -\ \includegraphics[valign,scale]{Figures/Equations/DashedPropagator.pdf}

which is the difference between the Feynman propagator and a disconnected (non-time-ordered) propagator:

\displaystyle\includegraphics[valign,scale]{Figures/Equations/CrossedPropagator.pdf}

\displaystyle\equiv\ \ \ G_{\text{F}}(k,\eta,\eta^{\prime})

\displaystyle=

\displaystyle{\displaystyle f}^{*}_{k}(\eta){f}_{k}(\eta^{\prime})\hskip 1.0pt\theta(\eta-\eta^{\prime})+{f}_{k}(\eta){f}^{*}_{k}(\eta^{\prime})\hskip 1.0pt\theta(\eta^{\prime}-\eta)\,,

(2.11)

\displaystyle\includegraphics[valign,scale]{Figures/Equations/DashedPropagator.pdf}

\displaystyle\equiv\ \ \ G_{\text{D}}(k,\eta,\eta^{\prime})

\displaystyle=

\displaystyle\frac{{f}^{*}_{k}(\eta_{*})}{f_{k}(\eta_{*})}f_{k}(\eta)f_{k}(\eta^{\prime})\,.

Note that the relative normalization is chosen so that the bulk-to-bulk propagator vanishes on the late-time boundary,
G(k,\eta,\eta_{*})=0
.

•

Vertices:
To each vertex
j
, we assign a (time-dependent) coupling
i\lambda_{j}\,a(\eta_{j})^{d+1}
and integrate over the interaction time
\eta_{j}
.

•

Loop integrals:
For diagrams involving loops, we integrate over the loop momenta.

As we will see, the mode functions of massive fields are Hankel functions so the wavefunction coefficients become nested integrals over products of these Hankel functions. Performing these integrals explicitly is challenging, so we will instead derive differential equations for an associated basis of master integrals.

Simplifying the wavefunction

It will be useful to extract some overall factors and write the mode function in (
2.5
) as
3
3

3

Here, we have used that
\nu
is either purely real or purely imaginary, so that

\left(e^{-i\frac{\pi\nu}{2}}H_{\nu}^{(2)}(-k\eta)\right)^{*}=e^{i\frac{\pi\nu}{2}}H_{\nu}^{(1)}(-k\eta)\,.

(2.12)

Moreover, the prefactor and
k
-scaling of the functions
g_{k}(\eta)
and
\bar{g}_{k}(\eta)
are chosen for later convenience.

\displaystyle f_{k}(\eta)

\displaystyle=i{H^{\frac{d-1}{2}}}\hskip 1.0pte^{-i\frac{\pi\nu}{2}}(-\eta)^{d/2-\nu}\,\frac{g_{k}(\eta)}{\sqrt{2k}}\,,

(2.13)

\displaystyle f_{k}^{*}(\eta)

\displaystyle=-i{H^{\frac{d-1}{2}}}\hskip 1.0pte^{+i\frac{\pi\nu}{2}}(-\eta)^{d/2-\nu}\,\frac{\bar{g}_{k}(\eta)}{\sqrt{2k}}\,,

where
we defined the new functions

\displaystyle g_{k}(\eta)

\displaystyle\equiv-i\sqrt{\frac{\pi}{2}}\,k^{-\xi}(-k\eta)^{\nu}H_{\nu}^{(2)}(-k\eta)\,,

(2.14)

\displaystyle\bar{g}_{k}(\eta)

\displaystyle\equiv i\sqrt{\frac{\pi}{2}}\,k^{-\xi}(-k\eta)^{\nu}H_{\nu}^{(1)}(-k\eta)\,.

Note that
\bar{g}_{k}(\eta)\neq g_{k}^{*}(\eta)
. Substituting (
2.13
) into (
2.9
) and (
2.11
), we find that the propagators are given by

\displaystyle K(k,\eta)

\displaystyle=N_{k}\hskip 1.0pt(-\eta)^{d/2-\nu}\,\hat{K}(k,\eta)\,,\qquad\qquad\ N_{k}\equiv\frac{i}{(-\eta_{*})^{d/2}H_{\nu}^{(2)}(-k\eta_{*})}\sqrt{\frac{2}{\pi k}}\,,

(2.15)

\displaystyle G_{\rm F}(k,\eta,\eta^{\prime})

\displaystyle=C_{k}^{({\rm F})}\hskip 1.0pt(\eta\eta^{\prime})^{d/2-\nu}\,\hat{G}_{\rm F}(k,\eta,\eta^{\prime})\,,\qquad\,C_{k}^{({\rm F})}\equiv\frac{H^{d-1}}{2k}\,,

\displaystyle G_{\rm D}(k,\eta,\eta^{\prime})

\displaystyle=C_{k}^{({\rm D})}\hskip 1.0pt(\eta\eta^{\prime})^{d/2-\nu}\,\hat{G}_{\rm D}(k,\eta,\eta^{\prime})\,,\qquad C_{k}^{({\rm D})}\equiv-\frac{H^{d-1}}{2k}\hskip 1.0pt\frac{H_{\nu}^{(1)}(-k\eta_{*})}{H_{\nu}^{(2)}(-k\eta_{*})}\,,

where we have defined the simplified propagators

\displaystyle\hat{K}(k,\eta)

\displaystyle\equiv g_{k}(\eta)\,,

(2.16)

\displaystyle\hat{G}_{\rm F}(k,\eta,\eta^{\prime})

\displaystyle\equiv\bar{g}_{k}(\eta){g}_{k}(\eta^{\prime})\hskip 1.0pt\theta(\eta-\eta^{\prime})+{g}_{k}(\eta)\bar{g}_{k}(\eta^{\prime})\hskip 1.0pt\theta(\eta^{\prime}-\eta)\,,

\displaystyle\hat{G}_{\rm D}(k,\eta,\eta^{\prime})

\displaystyle\equiv g_{k}(\eta)g_{k}(\eta^{\prime})\,.

We will compute a rescaled wavefunction
\hat{\psi}
using these rescaled propagators
\hat{K}
,
\hat{G}_{\rm F}
and
\hat{G}_{\rm D}
, because they will be somewhat simpler than the original objects.
To do this, we first absorb the additional factors of conformal time in
K,G
relative to
\hat{K},\hat{G}
into
modified vertex factors:

i\lambda_{i}\,a(\eta_{i})^{d+1}\prod_{j=1}^{p_{i}}(-\eta_{i})^{d/2-\nu_{j}}=i\lambda_{i}H^{-(d+1)}(-\eta_{i})^{-(1+\alpha_{i}+\xi_{i})}\,,

(2.17)

where we have defined the parameters

\alpha_{i}\equiv d-\frac{p_{i}}{2}(d-1)\quad{\rm and}\quad\xi_{i}\equiv\sum_{j=1}^{p_{i}}\left(\nu_{j}-\frac{1}{2}\right),

(2.18)

with
p_{i}
being the number of lines emanating from vertex
i
.
To derive the wavefunction coefficients coming from arbitrary graphs, we simply apply the Feynman rules of Section
2.2
, but with the rescaled propagators (
2.16
) and the modified vertex factors (
2.17
).
It is convenient to decompose the full answer into pieces and grade the various contributions by how many disconnected propagators appear in a given piece.
We denote these modified wavefunction coefficients by
\hat{\psi}^{(r)}
, where
r
counts the number of disconnected propagators.
The original wavefunction of interest can then be reassembled as

\psi\,=\,\sum_{r=0}^{n_{I}}\left(\prod_{e=1}^{n_{E}}N_{k_{e}}\prod_{i=1}^{n_{I}-r}C_{k_{I_{i}}}^{({\rm F})}\prod_{j=1}^{r}C_{k_{I_{j}}}^{({\rm D})}\,\hat{\psi}^{(r)}\right),

(2.19)

where
n_{E}
and
n_{I}
are the number of external and internal lines, respectively, and
k_{I_{i}}
are the internal momenta corresponding to either the Feynman (F) or disconnected (D) propagators.
In the rest of the paper, we omit the hat on
\hat{\psi}
, with the implicit understanding that we are always discussing the rescaled wavefunction.

2.3
Twisted Integrals

Applying the Feynman rules described in the previous section leads to a representation of the wavefunction coefficients as nested time integrals over products of Hankel functions. It is not obvious what the general features of such integrals are, or what kind of special functions they should evaluate to.
To gain further insight, it is therefore useful to recast the integrals of interest in a form where a broader range of mathematical tools can be applied.

Concretely, we would like to cast the time integrals of interest in a rational form, so that some results from geometry and combinatorics can be applied to them. To do so, we use the fact that Hankel functions admit an integral representation of the form

H_{\nu}^{(2)}(x)=\frac{i}{\sqrt{\pi}}\frac{2^{1+\nu}x^{-\nu}}{\Gamma[\tfrac{1}{2}-\nu]}\int_{1}^{\infty}{\rm d}t\,e^{-ixt}(t^{2}-1)^{-\nu-\frac{1}{2}}\,,

(2.20)

which expresses them as a twisted exponential integral.
The benefit of this representation is that it takes the same form regardless of the order
\nu
of the Hankel function, which only enters via the twist factor
(t^{2}-1)^{-\nu-\frac{1}{2}}
.
By substituting this expression (and its analogue for
H^{(1)}_{\nu}(x)
) into (
2.16
), and representing the temporal vertex factors in Fourier space, the time integrals only involve products of plane waves, and can be done explicitly.

After performing the time integrals, the wavefunction is expressed as an integral of a
universal integrand
times twist factors. As a concrete example, we consider the four-point function of conformally coupled scalar fields exchanging a field of general mass:

\displaystyle\psi

\displaystyle=\scalebox{1.0}{
\raisebox{-24.0pt}{

} }\,.

(2.21)

In Appendix
B
, we show that this
has the integral representation

\psi=\int\bigg(\prod_{a=1,2}{\rm d}x_{a}\,x_{a}^{\xi}\prod_{b=L,R}{\rm d}t_{b}\,(t_{b}^{2}-1)^{-\nu-\frac{1}{2}}\bigg)\,\uppsi(X_{a}+x_{a},t_{b}Y)\,,

(2.22)

where the rational function appearing inside the integral is
\uppsi\equiv\uppsi_{\rm F}-A\,\uppsi_{\rm D}
, with

\displaystyle\uppsi_{\rm F}

\displaystyle\equiv\frac{1}{2Y}\bigg[\frac{1}{X_{1}+X_{2}+(t_{L}-t_{R})Y}\frac{1}{X_{1}+t_{L}Y}+\frac{1}{X_{1}+X_{2}+(t_{R}-t_{L})Y}\frac{1}{X_{2}+t_{R}Y}\bigg]\,,

(2.23)

\displaystyle\uppsi_{\rm D}

\displaystyle\equiv\frac{1}{2Y}\,\frac{1}{X_{1}+t_{L}Y}\frac{1}{X_{2}+t_{R}Y}\,.

Note that, for
t_{L}=t_{R}\equiv 1
, this function reduces to the flat-space wavefunction. The relative normalization of the time-ordered (F) and disconnected (D) contributions is given by the parameter
A
. For heavy fields, this is a complex number, while, for light fields, it becomes
A=1
.
The universal integrand can also be written as

\uppsi\equiv\frac{1}{2Y}\frac{(1-A)(X_{1}+X_{2})^{2}+2(t_{L}X_{1}+t_{R}X_{2})Y+(1+A)(t_{L}-t_{R})^{2}Y^{2}}{(X_{1}+t_{L}Y)(X_{2}+t_{R}Y)(X_{1}+X_{2}+(t_{L}-t_{R})Y)(X_{1}+X_{2}+(t_{R}-t_{L})Y)}\,,

(2.24)

which makes its singularity structure manifest.
For more general external states (e.g. scalar fields of different masses), the integrand in (
2.22
) would remain the same; the only difference would be the way that we would integrate it.

The integrand (
2.24
), together with its generalizations to arbitrary bulk processes, admits an elegant definition in terms of combinatorial tubings of a decorated graph, with suggestive connections to underlying geometric structures. These features are briefly described in Appendix
B
. However, for our present purposes, the mere existence of a twisted integral representation like (
2.22
) is the most relevant fact. This structure of the integral means that we can apply the machinery of twisted cohomology
[
1
,
34
]
.

Integral basis

The geometric viewpoint implies
in particular that the wavefunction
\psi
is a member of a finite-dimensional vector space of integrals. This fact guarantees that it will satisfy a first-order matrix differential equation as a function of the external kinematics. The natural basis integrals have the same singularities as (
2.22
), but generalized to allow the twisted lines to have different parameters. We therefore consider integrals of the form
4
4

4

To write compact expressions like this, we have color-coded the signs in
\psi^{({\color[rgb]{0.8398,0.1523,0.1563}{\pm}}{\color[rgb]{0.1211,0.4648,0.707}{\pm}})}
. This will be even more relevant below. We hope that this does not cause any confusion in the black-and-white printing of this paper.

\psi^{({\color[rgb]{0.8398,0.1523,0.1563}{\pm}}{\color[rgb]{0.1211,0.4648,0.707}{\pm}})}\equiv\frac{1}{4}\int\bigg(\prod_{a=1,2}{\rm d}x_{a}\,x_{a}^{\xi}\prod_{b=L,R}{\rm d}t_{b}\,(t_{b}^{2}-1)^{-\nu-\frac{1}{2}}\bigg)\,(1\,{\color[rgb]{0.8398,0.1523,0.1563}{\mp}}\,t_{L})(1\,{\color[rgb]{0.1211,0.4648,0.707}{\pm}}\,t_{R})\,\uppsi^{(2)}(X_{a}+x_{a},t_{b}Y)\,.

(2.25)

These integrands shift the twists of the
(1\pm t_{L,R})
singularities by one unit, and so these integrals serve as a natural basis for this integral family.
The integrals (
2.25
) arise from replacing
g_{k}(\eta)
appearing in the propagator (
2.16
) with

\displaystyle g_{k}(\eta)\equiv h^{+}_{k}(\eta)+h^{-}_{k}(\eta)\,,\quad{\rm where}\quad h_{k}^{\pm}(\eta)

\displaystyle\equiv\frac{2^{\xi}}{\Gamma[-\xi]\,k^{\xi}}\int_{1}^{\infty}{\rm d}t\,e^{ik\eta t}\frac{1\,\pm\,t}{(t^{2}-1)^{1+\xi}}\,,

(2.26)

and similarly for
\bar{g}_{k}(\eta)\equiv\bar{h}^{+}_{k}(\eta)+\bar{h}^{-}_{k}(\eta)
. The benefit of this decomposition is that the functions
h_{k}^{\pm}(\eta)
satisfy a
first-order
differential equation in
\eta
, which leads to a simple first-order system for the basis functions
\psi^{(\pm\pm)}
. One recovers the original wavefunction by summing over all these basis elements as
\psi=\psi^{(++)}+\psi^{(--)}+\psi^{(+-)}+\psi^{(-+)}
.

3
Time for Differential Equations

Although the twisted integral representation is useful for establishing the
existence
of a first-order system of differential equations, the explicit derivation of these equations is most transparent in the time-integral representation.
In this section, we show how bulk perturbation theory naturally organizes the basis of master integrals and derive the differential equations that these integrals satisfy.
In doing so, we will find combinatorial patterns in the equations that we explore more fully in Section
4
.

3.1
Master Integrals

Perturbation theory in terms of
time
provides a natural organization of the basis of possible functions that arise in correlators. In
[
8
,
35
]
, this organization was used to derive a first-order system of differential equations satisfied by the wavefunction of conformally coupled scalars in power-law cosmologies. (See also
[
25
,
41
,
26
,
35
,
19
]
.)
In the present context, the existence of a first-order system is somewhat more surprising. In contrast to the conformal case
(where the mode functions are plane waves), the propagators (
2.16
) are assembled from mode functions that satisfy the
second-order
Klein–Gordon equation.

We can connect the twisted-integral and time-integral perspectives
by adding the time derivative of the mode function as a separate basis element. The time derivative of this function will then reduce back to the original mode function via the equation of motion. In particular, it is natural to consider the functions
[
22
,
21
]

h^{\pm}(x)=x^{\nu}H_{\nu}^{(2)}(x)\pm i\partial_{x}[x^{\nu}H_{\nu}^{(2)}(x)]=\frac{i}{\sqrt{\pi}}\frac{2^{1+\nu}}{\Gamma[\tfrac{1}{2}-\nu]}\int_{1}^{\infty}{\rm d}t\,e^{-ixt}\frac{1\pm t}{(t^{2}-1)^{\nu+\frac{1}{2}}}\,,

(3.1)

where in the last equality we have written this combination as a twisted integral, which is precisely (
2.26
). The functions
h^{\pm}
satisfy a
system of first-order equations

\partial_{x}h^{\pm}(x)\pm ih^{\pm}(x)\pm\frac{\nu-\tfrac{1}{2}}{x}\Big[h^{-}(x)-h^{+}(x)\Big]=0\,.

(3.2)

This suggests that we should try to build the basis of bulk integrals in terms of these combinations. The time-ordered structure of perturbation theory will then organize the differential system.

Concretely,
we first split each mode function
g_{k}(\eta)
appearing in (
2.14
)
into two auxiliary functions

\displaystyle g_{k}(\eta)\equiv h^{+}_{k}(\eta)+h^{-}_{k}(\eta)\,,\quad{\rm where}\quad h_{k}^{\pm}(\eta)

\displaystyle\equiv\frac{1}{2}\left(g_{k}(\eta)\mp\frac{i}{k}\partial_{\eta}g_{k}(\eta)\right),

(3.3)

and similarly for
\bar{g}_{k}(\eta)\equiv\bar{h}^{+}_{k}(\eta)+\bar{h}^{-}_{k}(\eta)
.
Up to a
k
-dependent factor, the functions
h_{k}^{\pm}
are equal to the functions
h^{\pm}
in (
3.2
), so that they satisfy the following first-order equations
5
5

5

Note that in (
3.5
) the term proportional to
\xi
is purely off-diagonal, which is a consequence of the
k^{-\xi}
factor in (
2.14
). This will simplify the resulting differential equations.

\displaystyle\partial_{\eta}h_{k}^{\pm}(\eta)

\displaystyle=\pm ikh_{k}^{\pm}(\eta)\pm\frac{\xi}{\eta}\left[h_{k}^{+}(\eta)-h_{k}^{-}(\eta)\right],

(3.4)

\displaystyle\partial_{k}h_{k}^{\pm}(\eta)

\displaystyle=\pm i\eta h_{k}^{\pm}(\eta)-\frac{\xi}{k}h_{k}^{\mp}(\eta)\,,

(3.5)

where again
\xi=\nu-\frac{1}{2}
. Identical equations hold for the functions
\bar{h}_{k}^{\pm}(\eta)
. We can then replace
g_{k}(\eta)
in the propagators (
2.16
) with
h^{\pm}_{k}(\eta)
, which effectively defines new propagators
\hat{K}^{\pm}
,
\hat{G}_{\rm F}^{\pm\pm}
and
\hat{G}_{\rm D}^{\pm\pm}
. We then use these propagators in the Feynman rules.
This separates the wavefunction
\psi
into a set of functions

\psi^{(\pm\pm\cdots\pm)}
assembled from strings of the functions
h_{k}^{\pm}(\eta)
and
\bar{h}_{k}^{\pm}(\eta)
. Since
h^{+}_{k}+h^{-}_{k}=g_{k}
, adding up all possible assignments of
\pm
in
\psi^{(\pm\pm\cdots\pm)}
reproduces the original function of interest
\psi
.

By taking time derivatives of the integrand and using (
3.4
) we will derive first-order
differential equations for the functions
\psi^{(\pm\pm\cdots\pm)}
, along with functions obtained by collapsing internal lines.
As in
[
8
]
, the equations separate into independent sectors graded by the number of disconnected propagators. Expressed in terms of the functions
h^{\pm}_{k}(\eta)
, each internal massive propagator leads to a four-fold multiplicity of basis functions, while each external line leads to an additional two-fold multiplicity. As an example, a
Feynman graph with a single massive exchange and conformally coupled external fields (with
\xi=0
) leads to four functions
\{\psi^{(++)}\,,\psi^{(+-)}\,,\psi^{(-+)}\,,\psi^{(--)}\}
in each of the time-ordered sector and the disconnected sector. In the time-ordered sector, the differential equations for
\psi^{(+-)}
and
\psi^{(-+)}
contain an additional source function
J^{(c)}
corresponding to a contact solution arising from the collapse of the propagator, so that there are
9
functions total.
6
6

6

Note that this is a substantial expansion of the size of the basis relative to
[
8
]
. We can understand this by noting that in the conformally coupled limit, half of the
h^{\pm}
functions vanish, and the other ones simplify

h^{-}_{k}(\eta)=\bar{h}^{+}_{k}(\eta)=0\,,\hskip 28.45274pt\,h^{+}_{k}(\eta)=\left(\bar{h}^{-}_{k}(\eta)\right)^{*}=e^{ik\eta}\,.

(3.6)

This reduces the size of the basis in the conformally coupled limit, and the corresponding differential equations and diagrammatic rules simplify to those of
[
8
]
.

In summary, to deal with time integrals over mode functions, we will increase the number of integrals by replacing each mode function with two auxiliary functions
h^{\pm}
. The benefit is that these satisfy a system of first-order differential equations. The desired original wavefunction coefficients can be recovered by adding up all the pieces of the new basis. In what follows, we illustrate this method by working out a few concrete examples.

3.2
Contact Diagram

We first study
a three-point contact diagram involving one generic massive leg and two conformally coupled legs. This is perhaps the simplest process involving a field of general mass. The wavefunction coefficient of interest is given by the integral

\psi_{c}\ \equiv\ \raisebox{-16.0pt}{
\hbox to58.91pt{\vbox to34.51pt{\pgfpicture\makeatletter\hbox{\hskip 29.45276pt\lower-2.20715pt\hbox to0.0pt{\lxSVG@begingroup@{_scopebegin} \lxSVG@begingroup@{stroke} \lxSVG@begingroup@{fill} \lxSVG@setlinewidth{\the\pgflinewidth}\lxSVG@begingroup@{stroke-width} \lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\nullfont\hbox to0.0pt{\lxSVG@begingroup@{_scopebegin} {{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces}}\lxSVG@setlinewidth{\the\pgflinewidth}\lxSVG@begingroup@{stroke-width} \lx@inpgf@ignorespaces
{}{{}}{}
{}{}\lxSVG@begingroup@{_scopebegin} \color[rgb]{0.75,0.75,0.75}\lxSVG@setlinewidth{\the\pgflinewidth}\lxSVG@begingroup@{stroke-width} \lx@inpgf@ignorespaces{}\lxSVG@stroke\lxSVG@drawpath@unclipped{M 0 0 L 0 43.31}{fill:none} \lx@inpgf@ignorespaces
\lxSVG@closescope {}{{}}{}
{}{}\lxSVG@begingroup@{_scopebegin} \color[rgb]{0.75,0.75,0.75}\lxSVG@setlinewidth{\the\pgflinewidth}\lxSVG@begingroup@{stroke-width} \lx@inpgf@ignorespaces{}\lxSVG@stroke\lxSVG@drawpath@unclipped{M 0 0 L 19.69 43.31}{fill:none} \lx@inpgf@ignorespaces
\lxSVG@closescope {}{{}}{}
{}{}\lxSVG@begingroup@{_scopebegin} \color[rgb]{0.25,0.25,0.25}\lxSVG@setlinewidth{\the\pgflinewidth}\lxSVG@begingroup@{stroke-width} \lx@inpgf@ignorespaces{}\lxSVG@stroke\lxSVG@drawpath@unclipped{M 0 0 L -19.69 43.31}{fill:none} \lx@inpgf@ignorespaces
\lxSVG@closescope {}{{}}{}
{}{}\lxSVG@begingroup@{_scopebegin} \color[rgb]{0.75,0.75,0.75}\lxSVG@setlinewidth{\the\pgflinewidth}\lxSVG@begingroup@{stroke-width} \lx@inpgf@ignorespaces{}\lxSVG@stroke\lxSVG@drawpath@unclipped{M -39.37 43.31 L 39.37 43.31}{fill:none} \lx@inpgf@ignorespaces
\lxSVG@closescope {}{{}}{}{{{}}{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces}{}{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces}{}{}{}{}{}}\lxSVG@begingroup@{_scopebegin} \lxSVG@begingroup@{fill} {}\lxSVG@fillstroke\lxSVG@drawpath@unclipped{M 0 0 M 2.36 0 C 2.36 1.3 1.3 2.36 0 2.36 C -1.3 2.36 -2.36 1.3 -2.36 0 C -2.36 -1.3 -1.3 -2.36 0 -2.36 C 1.3 -2.36 2.36 -1.3 2.36 0 Z M 0 0}{} \lx@inpgf@ignorespaces
\lxSVG@closescope
\lxSVG@closescope {\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces}{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces}{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces}\hss}\lxSVG@discardpath\lxSVG@closescope \hss}}\lxSVG@closescope\endpgfpicture}}
}=\int\frac{{\rm d}\eta}{(-\eta)^{1+\alpha+\xi}}\,e^{iX\eta}\,g_{k}(\eta)\,,

(3.7)

where
k\equiv k_{1}
and
X\equiv k_{2}+k_{3}
. To avoid clutter, we have dropped the overall normalization
N_{c}=i\lambda
. In this particular case, the time integral can be computed directly, and evaluates to a hypergeometric function. However, it is convenient to use this simplified setting to illustrate how integrals like this can be computed using differential equations.

Recall that we can decompose
g_{k}(\eta)=h^{+}_{k}(\eta)+h^{-}_{k}(\eta)
, which means that (
3.7
) can be split into two
basis functions:

\displaystyle\psi^{+}_{c}

\displaystyle=\int\frac{{\rm d}\eta}{(-\eta)^{1+\alpha+\xi}}\,e^{iX\eta}\,h^{+}_{k}(\eta)\,,

(3.8)

\displaystyle\psi^{-}_{c}

\displaystyle=\int\frac{{\rm d}\eta}{(-\eta)^{1+\alpha+\xi}}\,e^{iX\eta}\,h^{-}_{k}(\eta)\,,

where
\psi_{c}=\psi^{+}_{c}+\psi^{-}_{c}
.
In the inset below, we will show that these basis integrals satisfy the following differential equations:

{\rm d}\psi^{\pm}_{c}=\alpha\,{\rm d}\log(X\pm k)\,\psi^{\pm}_{c}\,+\,\xi\Big[{\rm d}\log(X\pm k)-{\rm d}\log k\Big]\psi^{\mp}_{c}\,,

(3.9)

where
{\rm d}={\rm d}X\hskip 1.0pt\partial_{X}+{\rm d}k\hskip 1.0pt\partial_{k}
is the differential with respect to kinematic variables. Notice that only dlog-forms of certain combinations of kinematic variables (called “letters”) appear in the differential.
It is also illuminating to write the differential equation as a matrix equation

{\rm d}\begin{bmatrix}\psi^{+}_{c}\\
\psi^{-}_{c}\end{bmatrix}=A\cdot\begin{bmatrix}\psi^{+}_{c}\\
\psi^{-}_{c}\end{bmatrix}\,,

(3.10)

where the “connection matrix” is

A=\alpha\begin{bmatrix}{\rm d}\log(X+k)&0\\
0&{\rm d}\log(X-k)\end{bmatrix}+\xi\begin{bmatrix}0&\ {\rm d}\log\left(\frac{X+k}{k}\right)\\
\ {\rm d}\log\left(\frac{X-k}{k}\right)&0\end{bmatrix}.

(3.11)

We see that
\xi\neq 0
induces off-diagonal mixings between the basis functions.

Derivation
: The derivation of equation (
3.9
) proceeds in two steps.

•

Shifted vertex factor
: First, we differentiate
\psi_{c}^{\pm}
with respect to
X
and
k
.
These derivatives can be brought inside the integrals and act on the mode functions. In cases where the momentum factors multiply
\eta
, these derivatives effectively raise the power of conformal time in the integral. This can also be thought of as shifting the vertex factor
\alpha
. For this reason, we make the dependence on
\alpha
explicit by writing
\psi^{\pm}_{c}(\alpha)
. First, we consider the derivative with respect to
X
:

\displaystyle\partial_{X}\psi^{\pm}_{c}(\alpha)

\displaystyle=\int\frac{{\rm d}\eta}{(-\eta)^{1+\alpha+\xi}}\,\partial_{X}\big[e^{iX\eta}\big]\,h^{\pm}_{k}(\eta)

\displaystyle=-i\int\frac{{\rm d}\eta}{(-\eta)^{\alpha+\xi}}\,e^{iX\eta}\,h^{\pm}_{k}(\eta)

\displaystyle=-i\psi^{\pm}_{c}(\alpha-1)\,.

(3.12)

To compute
\partial_{k}\psi^{\pm}_{c}(\alpha)
, we use (
3.5
), so that

\displaystyle\partial_{k}\psi^{\pm}_{c}(\alpha)

\displaystyle=\int\frac{{\rm d}\eta}{(-\eta)^{1+\alpha+\xi}}\,e^{iX\eta}\,\partial_{k}\big[h^{\pm}_{k}(\eta)\big]

\displaystyle=\mp i\psi^{\pm}_{c}(\alpha-1)-\frac{\xi}{k}\psi^{\mp}_{c}(\alpha)\,.

(3.13)

To find a closed system of equations, we need to find relations between the basis elements
\psi^{\pm}_{c}(\alpha)
and their counterparts
\psi^{\pm}_{c}(\alpha-1)
with a shifted vertex factor. Such relations follow from integration-by-parts identities.

•

Integration-by-parts
: Since the integral of a total derivative vanishes, we have

\displaystyle 0

\displaystyle=\int{\rm d}\eta\;\partial_{\eta}\big[{(-\eta)^{-\alpha-\xi}}e^{iX\eta}\,h^{\pm}_{k}(\eta)\big]

\displaystyle=(\alpha+\xi)\,\psi^{\pm}_{c}(\alpha)+\int\frac{{\rm d}\eta}{(-\eta)^{\alpha+\xi}}\partial_{\eta}\big[e^{iX\eta}\big]\,h^{\pm}_{k}(\eta)+\int\frac{{\rm d}\eta}{(-\eta)^{\alpha+\xi}}e^{iX\eta}\partial_{\eta}\big[h^{\pm}_{k}(\eta)\big]

\displaystyle=(\alpha+\xi)\,\psi^{\pm}_{c}(\alpha)+iX\psi^{\pm}_{c}(\alpha-1)\,\pm ik\psi^{\pm}_{c}(\alpha-1)-{\xi}\,\Big[\psi^{\pm}_{c}(\alpha)-\psi^{\mp}_{c}(\alpha)\Big]\,,

(3.14)

where we used (
3.4
) in the last equality.
We then use the identity (
3.14
) to replace
\psi^{\pm}_{c}(\alpha-1)
in (
•
‣
3.2
) and (
3.13
), so that

\displaystyle\partial_{X}\psi^{\pm}_{c}

\displaystyle=\frac{1}{X\pm k}\Big[\alpha\,\psi^{\pm}_{c}+\xi\,\psi^{\mp}_{c}\Big]\,,

(3.15)

\displaystyle\partial_{k}\psi^{\pm}_{c}

\displaystyle=\pm\frac{1}{X\pm k}\Big[\alpha\,\psi^{\pm}_{c}+\xi\,\psi^{\mp}_{c}\Big]-\frac{\xi}{k}\,\psi^{\mp}_{c}\,,

which leads to (
3.9
) in terms of differential forms.

The system of equations (
3.10
) is two-dimensional, which implies that each of the basis elements (and their sum) satisfy a second-order differential equation. Indeed, combining the equations for
\psi_{c}^{\pm}
, it is easy to show that
\psi_{c}=\psi_{c}^{+}+\psi_{c}^{-}
satisfies

\Big[\left(X^{2}-k^{2}\right)\partial_{X}^{2}+2X(1-\alpha)\partial_{X}-(\alpha+\xi)(1-\alpha+\xi)\Big]\psi_{c}=0\,,

(3.16)

which has the following solution

\psi_{c}=A(\xi,\alpha)\,(2k)^{\alpha}\,{}_{2}F_{1}\bigg[\begin{array}[]{c}-\alpha-\xi\ ,\ 1-\alpha+\xi\\[-1.0pt]
1-\alpha\end{array}\bigg\rvert\,\frac{k-X}{2k}\,\bigg]\,,

(3.17)

where we imposed regularity of the wavefunction at
k=X
, and the
k^{\alpha}
prefactor follows from dilation invariance.
7
7

7

In checking this, recall that
N_{k}\sim k^{\xi}
, and the physical wavefunction has dimension
\nu+1-d/2
.
The overall normalization

A(\xi,\alpha)

can be fixed by directly evaluating the integral in (
3.7
) for a specific value of
k
.

Notice that this involves a new source function

\displaystyle J_{\hskip-1.22911pt\raisebox{-2.2604pt}{\includegraphics[scale]{Figures/Equations/Collapsed.pdf}}}^{(c)}\equiv\int\frac{{\rm d}\eta}{(-\eta)^{1+\alpha_{1}+\alpha_{2}}}\,e^{i(X_{1}+X_{2})\eta}\,.

(3.26)

This term arises from collapsing the bulk-to-bulk propagator, which produces a contact diagram with conformally coupled external lines.
The differential of the new source function is

\displaystyle{\rm d}J_{\hskip-1.22911pt\raisebox{-2.2604pt}{\includegraphics[scale]{Figures/Equations/Collapsed.pdf}}}^{(c)}

\displaystyle=(\alpha_{1}+\alpha_{2})L\,J_{\hskip-1.22911pt\raisebox{-2.2604pt}{\includegraphics[scale]{Figures/Equations/Collapsed.pdf}}}^{(c)}\,,

(3.27)

where
L\equiv{\rm d}\log(X_{1}+X_{2})
. Hence, the system closes with the addition of this function.

which follows from the Wronskian of the Hankel functions.

Finally, the derivatives of the collapsed source term can be derived directly from its definition (
3.37
):

\displaystyle\partial_{X_{1}}J_{\hskip-1.22911pt\raisebox{-2.2604pt}{\includegraphics[scale]{Figures/Equations/Collapsed.pdf}}}^{(c)}=\partial_{X_{2}}J_{\hskip-1.22911pt\raisebox{-2.2604pt}{\includegraphics[scale]{Figures/Equations/Collapsed.pdf}}}^{(c)}

\displaystyle=\frac{\alpha_{1}+\alpha_{2}}{X_{1}+X_{2}}J_{\hskip-1.22911pt\raisebox{-2.2604pt}{\includegraphics[scale]{Figures/Equations/Collapsed.pdf}}}^{(c)}\,,

(3.41)

\displaystyle\partial_{Y}J_{\hskip-1.22911pt\raisebox{-2.2604pt}{\includegraphics[scale]{Figures/Equations/Collapsed.pdf}}}^{(c)}

\displaystyle=0\,.

Combining these partial derivatives, we obtain equation (
3.27
) in terms of the total differential.
The explicit solution for this source term is

J_{\hskip-1.22911pt\raisebox{-2.2604pt}{\includegraphics[scale]{Figures/Equations/Collapsed.pdf}}}^{(c)}=c_{\hskip-1.22911pt\raisebox{-2.2604pt}{\includegraphics[scale]{Figures/Equations/Collapsed.pdf}}}\hskip 1.0pt(X_{1}+X_{2})^{\alpha_{1}+\alpha_{2}}\,,\quad{\rm with}\quad c_{\hskip-1.22911pt\raisebox{-2.2604pt}{\includegraphics[scale]{Figures/Equations/Collapsed.pdf}}}\equiv\hskip 1.0pti^{\alpha_{1}+\alpha_{2}}\hskip 1.0pt\Gamma(-\alpha_{1}-\alpha_{2})\,,

(3.42)

where the overall normalization is found by direct integration of (
3.37
).

In
[
6
,
4
]
, a
second-order
differential equation was derived for the massive exchange graph:

\Big[\left(X_{1}^{2}-Y^{2}\right)\partial_{X_{1}}^{2}+2X_{1}(1-\alpha_{1})\partial_{X_{1}}-(\alpha_{1}+\xi)(1-\alpha_{1}+\xi)\Big]\psi_{e}^{(2)}=d(Y)(X_{1}+X_{2})^{\alpha_{1}+\alpha_{2}-1}\,,

(3.43)

where
d(Y)
is independent of
X_{1},X_{2}
. This equation can be viewed as a consequence of the wave equation obeyed by the bulk Green’s functions.
Let us confirm that this equation can be recovered from our system of first-order equations.

3.4
Double Exchange

The single-exchange example that we just discussed already displays essentially all of the complexities of the general case. Nevertheless, in order to see the general pattern, it is useful to consider an additional example.

(3.48)

The total energy flowing from vertex
i
to the boundary is denoted by
X_{i}
and the energies exchanged between the vertices are labeled
Y
and
Y^{\prime}
.
Since the propagators do not necessarily correspond to fields with the same mass, we use
\xi
and
\xi^{\prime}
for the weight parameters of each propagator. We also define
\xi_{1}\equiv\xi
,
\xi_{2}\equiv\xi+\xi^{\prime}
and
\xi_{3}\equiv\xi^{\prime}
, which appear as powers in the vertex factors.

For simplicity,
we consider only the fully time-ordered contribution. The disconnected contributions can be related to the single-exchange and contact examples we have already considered.
Using the Feynman rules presented in Section
2
, the connected wavefunction coefficient (
3.48
) is given by the following integral

\psi_{e}^{(3)}=\int\left[\prod_{i=1}^{3}\frac{{\rm d}\eta_{i}}{(-\eta_{i})^{1+\alpha_{i}+\xi_{i}}}\,e^{iX_{i}\eta_{i}}\right]\,\hat{G}_{\text{F}}(Y,\eta_{1},\eta_{2})\hskip 1.0pt\hat{G}_{\text{F}}(Y^{\prime},\eta_{2},\eta_{3})\,.

(3.49)

We separate this into
16
basis functions by substituting the mode functions
g_{Y}(\eta)=h^{+}_{Y}(\eta)+h^{-}_{Y}(\eta)
and
\bar{g}_{Y}(\eta)=\bar{h}^{+}_{Y}(\eta)+\bar{h}^{-}_{Y}(\eta)
.
Each bulk-to-bulk propagator then separates into four parts:

\hat{G}_{\text{F}}^{({\color[rgb]{0.8398,0.1523,0.1563}{\pm}}{\color[rgb]{0.582,0,0.8281}\pm})}(Y,\eta_{1},\eta_{2})\equiv\bar{h}^{{\color[rgb]{0.8398,0.1523,0.1563}{\pm}}}_{Y}(\eta_{1})h^{{\color[rgb]{0.582,0,0.8281}\pm}}_{Y}(\eta_{2})\,\theta_{12}+h^{{\color[rgb]{0.8398,0.1523,0.1563}{\pm}}}_{Y}(\eta_{1})\bar{h}^{{\color[rgb]{0.582,0,0.8281}\pm}}_{Y}(\eta_{2})\,\theta_{21}\,,

(3.50)

so that (
3.49
) can be expressed as the sum of the following functions

\psi^{({\color[rgb]{0.8398,0.1523,0.1563}{\pm}}{\color[rgb]{0.582,0,0.8281}\pm_{1}})({\color[rgb]{0.582,0,0.8281}\pm_{2}}{\color[rgb]{0.1211,0.4648,0.707}{\pm}})}=\int\left[\prod_{i=1}^{3}\frac{{\rm d}\eta_{i}}{(-\eta_{i})^{1+\alpha_{i}+\xi_{i}}}\,e^{iX_{i}\eta_{i}}\right]\,\hat{G}_{\text{F}}^{({\color[rgb]{0.8398,0.1523,0.1563}{\pm}}{\color[rgb]{0.582,0,0.8281}\pm_{1}})}(Y,\eta_{1},\eta_{2})\hskip 1.0pt\hat{G}_{\text{F}}^{({\color[rgb]{0.582,0,0.8281}\pm_{2}}{\color[rgb]{0.1211,0.4648,0.707}{\pm}})}(Y^{\prime},\eta_{2},\eta_{3})\,.

(3.51)

Applying the same procedure as in the previous examples, one can straightforwardly derive the differential of these basis functions:

\displaystyle{\rm d}\psi^{({\color[rgb]{0.8398,0.1523,0.1563}{\pm}}{\color[rgb]{0.582,0,0.8281}\pm_{1}})({\color[rgb]{0.582,0,0.8281}\pm_{2}}{\color[rgb]{0.1211,0.4648,0.707}{\pm}})}

\displaystyle=\Big[\alpha_{1}\ell^{{\color[rgb]{0.8398,0.1523,0.1563}{\pm}}}_{1}+\alpha_{2}\ell^{{\color[rgb]{0.582,0,0.8281}\pm_{1}}{\color[rgb]{0.582,0,0.8281}\pm_{2}}}_{2}+\alpha_{3}\ell^{{\color[rgb]{0.1211,0.4648,0.707}{\pm}}}_{3}\Big]\,\psi^{({\color[rgb]{0.8398,0.1523,0.1563}{\pm}}{\color[rgb]{0.582,0,0.8281}\pm_{1}})({\color[rgb]{0.582,0,0.8281}\pm_{2}}{\color[rgb]{0.1211,0.4648,0.707}{\pm}})}

(3.52)

\displaystyle+\xi\hskip 1.0pt(\ell^{{\color[rgb]{0.8398,0.1523,0.1563}{\pm}}}_{1}-L_{12})\hskip 1.0pt\psi^{({\color[rgb]{0.8398,0.1523,0.1563}{\mp}}{\color[rgb]{0.582,0,0.8281}\pm_{1}})({\color[rgb]{0.582,0,0.8281}\pm_{2}}{\color[rgb]{0.1211,0.4648,0.707}{\pm}})}+\xi\hskip 1.0pt(\ell^{{\color[rgb]{0.582,0,0.8281}\pm_{1}}{\color[rgb]{0.582,0,0.8281}\pm_{2}}}_{2}-L_{12})\psi^{({\color[rgb]{0.8398,0.1523,0.1563}{\pm}}{\color[rgb]{0.582,0,0.8281}\mp_{1}})({\color[rgb]{0.582,0,0.8281}\pm_{2}}{\color[rgb]{0.1211,0.4648,0.707}{\pm}})}

\displaystyle+\xi^{\prime}(\ell^{{\color[rgb]{0.1211,0.4648,0.707}{\pm}}}_{3}-L_{23})\hskip 1.0pt\psi^{({\color[rgb]{0.8398,0.1523,0.1563}{\pm}}{\color[rgb]{0.582,0,0.8281}\pm_{1}})({\color[rgb]{0.582,0,0.8281}\pm_{2}}{\color[rgb]{0.1211,0.4648,0.707}{\mp}})}+\xi^{\prime}(\ell^{{\color[rgb]{0.582,0,0.8281}\pm_{1}}{\color[rgb]{0.582,0,0.8281}\pm_{2}}}_{2}-L_{23})\hskip 1.0pt\psi^{({\color[rgb]{0.8398,0.1523,0.1563}{\pm}}{\color[rgb]{0.582,0,0.8281}\pm_{1}})({\color[rgb]{0.582,0,0.8281}\mp_{2}}{\color[rgb]{0.1211,0.4648,0.707}{\pm}})}

\displaystyle-\frac{({\color[rgb]{0.8398,0.1523,0.1563}\pm\,1}\,{\color[rgb]{0.582,0,0.8281}\mp_{1}\,1})}{2}(\ell^{{\color[rgb]{0.8398,0.1523,0.1563}{\pm}}}_{1}-\ell^{{\color[rgb]{0.582,0,0.8281}\pm_{1}}{\color[rgb]{0.582,0,0.8281}\pm_{2}}}_{2})\hskip 1.0ptJ^{(c)({\color[rgb]{0.582,0,0.8281}\pm_{2}}{\color[rgb]{0.1211,0.4648,0.707}{\pm}})}-\frac{({\color[rgb]{0.1211,0.4648,0.707}\pm\,1}\,{\color[rgb]{0.582,0,0.8281}\mp_{2}\,1})}{2}(\ell^{{\color[rgb]{0.1211,0.4648,0.707}{\pm}}}_{3}-\ell^{{\color[rgb]{0.582,0,0.8281}\pm_{1}}{\color[rgb]{0.582,0,0.8281}\pm_{2}}}_{2})\hskip 1.0ptJ^{({\color[rgb]{0.8398,0.1523,0.1563}{\pm}}{\color[rgb]{0.582,0,0.8281}\pm_{1}})(c)}\,,

where we have defined the following shorthand for the dlog-forms that appear:

\displaystyle\ell_{1}^{{\color[rgb]{0.8398,0.1523,0.1563}{\pm}}}

\displaystyle={\rm d}\log(X_{1}\,{\color[rgb]{0.8398,0.1523,0.1563}{\pm}}\,Y)\,,

\displaystyle\qquad L_{12}

\displaystyle={\rm d}\log Y\,,

(3.53)

\displaystyle\ell_{3}^{{\color[rgb]{0.1211,0.4648,0.707}{\pm}}}

\displaystyle={\rm d}\log(X_{3}\,{\color[rgb]{0.1211,0.4648,0.707}{\pm}}\,Y^{\prime})\,,

\displaystyle\qquad L_{23}

\displaystyle={\rm d}\log Y^{\prime}\,,

\displaystyle\ell_{2}^{{\color[rgb]{0.582,0,0.8281}\pm_{1}}{\color[rgb]{0.582,0,0.8281}\pm_{2}}}

\displaystyle={\rm d}\log(X_{2}\,{\color[rgb]{0.582,0,0.8281}\pm_{1}}\,Y\,{\color[rgb]{0.582,0,0.8281}\pm_{2}}\,Y^{\prime})\,.

Despite the apparent complexity of (
3.52
), there is a simple pattern in these equations.
The source terms in the first line are simply the original functions, while the functions appearing in the second and third lines (proportional to
\xi
and
\xi^{\prime}
) can be obtained from all possible sign flips of a single entry in the superscript of
\psi^{({\color[rgb]{0.8398,0.1523,0.1563}{\pm}}{\color[rgb]{0.582,0,0.8281}\pm_{1}})({\color[rgb]{0.582,0,0.8281}\pm_{2}}{\color[rgb]{0.1211,0.4648,0.707}{\pm}})}
. The letters multiplying these source functions are correlated with these sign flips. Finally, in the last line, new functions
J^{(c)({\color[rgb]{0.582,0,0.8281}\pm_{2}}{\color[rgb]{0.1211,0.4648,0.707}{\pm}})}
and
J^{({\color[rgb]{0.8398,0.1523,0.1563}{\pm}}{\color[rgb]{0.582,0,0.8281}\pm_{1}})(c)}
appear, which arise from collapsing either the left or right propagator.

The functions with a single collapsed propagator are closely related to the functions appearing in the two-site wavefunction discussed in Section
3.3
. For example, we can write
J^{({\color[rgb]{0.8398,0.1523,0.1563}{\pm}}{\color[rgb]{0.582,0,0.8281}\pm_{1}})(c)}
as

The differential of this function is

where

.

The differential equations that we found are more structured than one would have anticipated. Indeed, we saw that the equations obtained by integration-by-parts can be understood in terms of sign flips and collapsing propagators of the underlying Feynman graph. This provides a simple “binary” interpretation of the differential equations for these functions, which is simply related to the pattern of sign flips. This pattern can be straightforwardly extended to arbitrary graphs.
In order to do so, it is convenient to encode the differential equations pictorially, which makes
the combinatorial features of these equations more manifest.

4
Circling Back to the Boundary

Looking at the differential equations derived in Section
3
suggests a simple organizing structure.
In
[
2
,
8
]
, a similar pattern was discovered for the differential equations of conformally coupled fields in power-law cosmologies.
This became especially vivid when both the basis functions and the letters of the differential equations were represented combinatorially in terms of graph tubings. These tubings “evolve” as one takes derivatives, subject to simple rules. This recasting of the evolution of the wavefunction as dynamics through the combinatorics of kinematic variables was called “kinematic flow”
[
2
,
3
]
.

In this section, we will show that a similar kinematic flow description also exists for fields with generic masses in de Sitter space. In fact, there is a sense in which the construction is even more natural for the massive case. As we saw in Section
3
, the differential equations are essentially determined by patterns of sign flips, and so it is not very surprising that this procedure has a simple combinatorial description.
Like in
[
8
]
, the differential equations separate into independent sectors graded by the number of disconnected propagators. For simplicity, we will therefore restrict our discussion to fully connected graphs
(with only Feynman propagators). The equations for the contributions with disconnected propagators can be obtained from the equations for the fully time-ordered subgraphs.

4.1
Marked Graphs and Tubings

We start by introducing the concept of “truncated graphs.” This means removing all conformally coupled (gray) external lines and only keeping track of the energies associated to these lines. For example, we would truncate the following graphs:

\raisebox{-25.0pt}{
\hbox to178.41pt{\vbox to57.52pt{\pgfpicture\makeatletter\hbox{\hskip 29.45276pt\lower-11.86847pt\hbox to0.0pt{\lxSVG@begingroup@{_scopebegin} \lxSVG@begingroup@{stroke} \lxSVG@begingroup@{fill} \lxSVG@setlinewidth{\the\pgflinewidth}\lxSVG@begingroup@{stroke-width} \lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\nullfont\hbox to0.0pt{\lxSVG@begingroup@{_scopebegin} {{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces}}\lxSVG@setlinewidth{\the\pgflinewidth}\lxSVG@begingroup@{stroke-width} \lx@inpgf@ignorespaces
{}{{}}{}
{}{}\lxSVG@begingroup@{_scopebegin} \color[rgb]{0.75,0.75,0.75}\lxSVG@setlinewidth{\the\pgflinewidth}\lxSVG@begingroup@{stroke-width} \lx@inpgf@ignorespaces{}\lxSVG@stroke\lxSVG@drawpath@unclipped{M 0 0 L 0 43.31}{fill:none} \lx@inpgf@ignorespaces
\lxSVG@closescope {}{{}}{}

(4.2)

This is natural from the bulk perspective because the mode functions of conformally coupled scalars are plane waves, so the energies flowing in/out of vertices just add together.
From these truncated graphs, we then create “marked graphs” by adding crosses on all the remaining lines (internal and external). The letters (singularities) of the differential equations, as well as the basis functions, can then be represented graphically as “tubings” of these marked graphs.

Letters

The letters of the differential equations are in one-to-one correspondence with ‘‘tubes”---connected proper subgraphs, represented by
encircling the vertices and crosses---on the marked graph.
To each tube we assign a combination of kinematic variables given by the sum of vertex energies enclosed by the tube and the energies of the lines piercing the tube.
For tubes that intersect a line and enclose the corresponding cross, one flips the sign of the energy associated to that line.

The singularities for more complicated graphs are the obvious generalizations of the singularities (tubes) shown in (
4.3
) and (
4.4
).

Functions

The functions in the differential system are also in one-to-one correspondence with graphical objects. Each function can be represented by a “complete tubing” of the marked graph, where each vertex is included in exactly one tube.
The crosses on massive propagators can be in multiple overlapping tubes. It is best to illustrate this with some examples.

•

Single exchange:

(4.5)

This is a graphical encoding of all possible assignments of a pair of
+
or
-
signs to the internal line, matching the possible propagator splits discussed in Section
3.1
. We
assign a minus sign when a tube encircles the corresponding cross and a plus sign when it does not.
Completely enclosing an internal line like in
J^{(c)}
corresponds to collapsing the propagator.

•

Contact diagram:

As a simple example with a massive external line, we consider a

Conformal limit

In
[
8
]
, similar graph tubings were introduced to represent the basis functions for theories with conformally coupled fields in a power-law cosmology. In the case of massive propagators, we have additional basis functions and their graphical representations have a slightly different meaning. To prevent confusion, we briefly highlight the difference in notation and discuss the conformal limit of the basis functions introduced in this work.

•

Single exchange:
We first look at the two-site graph with a single massive exchange.
In that case, the basis functions were represented graphically in (
4.5
) and algebraically in
(
3.21
):

\psi^{({\color[rgb]{0.8398,0.1523,0.1563}{\pm}}{\color[rgb]{0.1211,0.4648,0.707}{\pm}})}=\int{\rm d}\eta_{1}{\rm d}\eta_{2}\,\frac{e^{iX_{1}\eta_{1}}e^{iX_{2}\eta_{2}}}{(-\eta_{1})^{1+\alpha_{1}+\xi}(-\eta_{2})^{1+\alpha_{2}+\xi}}\Big[\bar{h}^{{\color[rgb]{0.8398,0.1523,0.1563}{\pm}}}_{Y}(\eta_{1})h^{{\color[rgb]{0.1211,0.4648,0.707}{\pm}}}_{Y}(\eta_{2})\,\theta_{12}+h^{{\color[rgb]{0.8398,0.1523,0.1563}{\pm}}}_{Y}(\eta_{1})\bar{h}^{{\color[rgb]{0.1211,0.4648,0.707}{\pm}}}_{Y}(\eta_{2})\,\theta_{21}\Big]\,.

(4.7)

We recall that in the conformal limit
h_{k}^{-}=\bar{h}_{k}^{+}=0
, so that
\psi^{(++)}=\psi^{(--)}\to 0
.

and

and

\mathbin{\hbox to3.57pt{\vbox to3.57pt{\pgfpicture\makeatletter\hbox{\hskip 0.43056pt\lower-0.43056pt\hbox to0.0pt{\lxSVG@begingroup@{_scopebegin} \lxSVG@begingroup@{stroke} \lxSVG@begingroup@{fill} \lxSVG@setlinewidth{\the\pgflinewidth}\lxSVG@begingroup@{stroke-width} \lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\nullfont\hbox to0.0pt{\lxSVG@begingroup@{_scopebegin} {\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces}\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces}\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\lxSVG@setlinewidth{\the\pgflinewidth}\lxSVG@begingroup@{stroke-width} \lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\color[rgb]{0,0,0}{}{{}}{}

, respectively.
It is interesting to see that, for generic masses, these functions contain
a mixture of the two possible time orderings. In the conformal limit, however, half of each function vanishes and we get

\displaystyle\psi^{(+-)}

\displaystyle\longrightarrow\,\psi_{\includegraphics[]{Figures/Equations/psi-.pdf}}\,,

(4.8)

\displaystyle\psi^{(-+)}

\displaystyle\longrightarrow\,\psi_{\includegraphics[]{Figures/Equations/psi+.pdf}}\,,

so that the basis functions reduce to their (anti)time-ordered contributions.

We see that two phenomena happen in the conformal limit. First, the size of the basis decreases because some functions identically vanish. Second, the remaining functions have a definite time ordering, which importantly is not the case away from the conformally coupled limit. These two features persist in more general examples.

•

Contact diagram:
The basis functions for a contact diagram with a single massive leg were represented graphically in (
4.6
) and algebraically in (
3.8
):

\psi^{\pm}_{c}=\int\frac{{\rm d}\eta}{(-\eta)^{1+\alpha+\xi}}\,e^{iX\eta}\,h^{\pm}_{k}(\eta)\,.

(4.9)

It is trivial to see that in the conformal limit, where
h^{-}_{k}\to 0
and
h^{+}_{k}\to e^{ik\eta}
, we have
\psi^{-}_{c}\to 0
and only
\psi_{c}^{+}
survives. This is consistent with the fact that, in the conformal case, we have a unique basis function with energy
X+k
.

\lxSVG@closescope {{

\displaystyle{\rm d}J_{\includegraphics[scale]{Figures/Tubings/Functions/psic.pdf}}

\displaystyle\,=\,(\alpha_{1}+\alpha_{2})\,\includegraphics[scale,valign]{Figures/Tubings/two/Lab.pdf}\ J_{\includegraphics[scale]{Figures/Tubings/Functions/psic.pdf}}\,.

(4.13)

Again, the contributions in the first line of each expression are the same as in the conformally coupled case
[
8
]
, while the second line contains new terms coming from the massive propagator.
This pictorial representation efficiently encodes the pattern of signs and letters appearing in (
3.25
).

Flow rules

In Section
3
, we saw that the system of differential equations satisfied by the functions
\psi^{(\pm\cdots\pm)}
are simply related to the signs of the functions and the pattern of collapsing internal lines. These equations can be derived by systematically applying integration-by-parts identities and shift relations. We have also seen that the results can be given a simple graphical representation in terms of tubings of the corresponding graphs. We now explain that the equations can also be derived from a set of simple rules that govern the growth of graph tubings through the differential system.

The starting point is the graph tubing associated to a specific “parent function” of interest. As an illustration, we will take the function
\psi_{\includegraphics[scale]{Figures/Tubings/Functions/psi-.pdf}}
, whose differential appears in (
4.10
). This differential follows from three simple steps.

1.

Activation
: Each tube of the graph tubing gets “activated” and becomes a letter in the differential equation.
The letter is multiplied by the function corresponding to the original graph times the sum of the parameters
\alpha_{i}
associated to its enclosed vertices. This generates the first term on the right-hand side of
(
4.10
):

{\rm d}\psi_{\includegraphics[scale]{Figures/Tubings/Functions/psi-.pdf}}\,\supset\,\Big(\alpha_{1}\,\includegraphics[scale,valign]{Figures/Tubings/two/Lam.pdf}\,+\,\alpha_{2}\includegraphics[scale,valign]{Figures/Tubings/two/Lbp.pdf}\Big)\,\psi_{\includegraphics[scale]{Figures/Tubings/Functions/psi-.pdf}}\ .

(4.14)

2.

Merger
: If the graph tubing has tubes that are adjacent to each other, these tubes can “merge” to form a larger tube.
The function associated to this new tubing will appear as a source function in the differential equation. This source function multiplies the
difference
of the two letters corresponding to the two tubes involved in the merger. The letter containing the cross on the merged edge appears with a plus sign. This explains the second term on the right-hand side of
(
4.10
):

{\rm d}\psi_{\includegraphics[scale]{Figures/Tubings/Functions/psi-.pdf}}\,\supset\,\Big(\alpha_{1}\,\includegraphics[scale,valign]{Figures/Tubings/two/Lam.pdf}\,+\,\alpha_{2}\includegraphics[scale,valign]{Figures/Tubings/two/Lbp.pdf}\Big)\,\psi_{\includegraphics[scale]{Figures/Tubings/Functions/psi-.pdf}}\,+\,\Big(\includegraphics[scale,valign]{Figures/Tubings/two/Lam.pdf}\,-\,\includegraphics[scale,valign]{Figures/Tubings/two/Lbp.pdf}\Big)\,J_{\includegraphics[scale]{Figures/Tubings/Functions/psic.pdf}}\ .

(4.15)

If the theory contains only conformally coupled fields, this generates the full differential
[
8
]
.
To capture massive propagators, however, we need one additional rule.

3.

Mixing
: Tubes that are pierced by massive propagators (lines with crosses on them) can
grow
and
shrink
to produce new source functions. The new source functions multiply the
difference
of the letter corresponding to the
changed tube and the letter of the relevant internal line, times the parameter
\xi
describing the massive field.
This completes the derivation of the differential in (
4.10
):

\displaystyle{\rm d}\psi_{\includegraphics[scale]{Figures/Tubings/Functions/psi-.pdf}}

\displaystyle=\,\Big(\alpha_{1}\,\includegraphics[scale,valign]{Figures/Tubings/two/Lam.pdf}\,+\,\alpha_{2}\includegraphics[scale,valign]{Figures/Tubings/two/Lbp.pdf}\Big)\,\psi_{\includegraphics[scale]{Figures/Tubings/Functions/psi-.pdf}}\,+\,\Big(\includegraphics[scale,valign]{Figures/Tubings/two/Lam.pdf}\,-\,\includegraphics[scale,valign]{Figures/Tubings/two/Lbp.pdf}\Big)\,J_{\includegraphics[scale]{Figures/Tubings/Functions/psic.pdf}}

(4.16)

\displaystyle+\xi\,\Big[\Big(\includegraphics[scale,valign]{Figures/Tubings/two/Lam.pdf}-\raisebox{3.0pt}{

The first term in the second line arises from the shrinking of the left tube, while the second term comes from the growth of the right tube.

By systematically applying these three rules, one can derive the differential equations for arbitrary Feynman graphs with massive propagators.

4.3
Selected Examples

To make the application of these rules more concrete, we now illustrate them in a few examples.
The examples in this section involve specific tree diagrams, but the algorithm works for arbitrary graphs (including diagrams with loops), without modification. We provide an explicit application to the simplest one-loop case in Appendix
C
.

Double exchange

As a slightly more complex example than the single exchange considered in Section
4.2
, let us describe the
double exchange of massive fields, with conformally coupled external lines, as studied in Section
3.4
.
First, we note that the list of letters is identical to the conformally coupled case
[
8
]

\displaystyle\includegraphics[scale,valign]{Figures/Tubings/three/LLap.pdf}\ \equiv\ {\rm d}\log(X_{1}+Y)\,,

\displaystyle\includegraphics[scale,valign]{Figures/Tubings/three/LLam.pdf}\ \equiv\ {\rm d}\log(X_{1}-Y)\,,

The first term (proportional to
\alpha
) arises from the standard activation of the tube to produce the corresponding letter. The second term (proportional to
\xi_{1}
) has a new source function created by the shrinking tube, while the third and fourth terms (proportional to
\xi_{2}
and
\xi_{3}
) come from growing the tube onto the second and third legs, respectively.

One can follow the same procedure for the other basis elements. The resulting system of first-order equations can be shown to imply the conformal Ward identities satisfied by the three-point function of massive fields
[
24
,
18
]
.

5
Massive Solutions to Massive Problems

In the previous two sections, we derived differential equations for wavefunction coefficients with massive propagators and identified an interesting combinatorial structure in these equations.
In this section, we consider the systematics of obtaining solutions to these equations.

For concreteness, we will focus on the simplest case of a single massive exchange between conformally coupled fields. The relevant differential equations for the connected component are

where

with a constant coefficient

.
Different values of
\alpha_{i}
correspond to different
n
-point functions, where the number of fields involved in each vertex determines
\alpha_{i}
via (
2.18
). We are interested in the four-point function in
d=3
, so that
\alpha_{i}\to 0
.
While the correlator for this process can be written as a generalized hypergeometric series for any mass parameter
[
4
]
, the first-order equations (
5.1
) are especially well suited to an analysis in the parametric regimes where the mass of the exchanged particle is taken either to infinity or to the conformal value.
We will therefore derive solutions to these equations in the limits of light (
\xi\to 0
) and heavy (
\xi\to\infty
) particle exchange.

5.1
Light Particle Exchange

We first consider the case of light particle exchange, where the mass of the exchanged particle is close to the conformally coupled value
\nu=\tfrac{1}{2}
.
The solution can then be organized as a perturbative expansion in the small parameter
\xi\to 0
, so that each function in (
5.1
) is

\psi^{(\pm\pm)}_{\hskip-1.63885pt\raisebox{0.3014pt}{\resizebox{1356540}{}{

(5.2)

We then solve
the equations order by order in

. At each order in the expansion, the functions satisfy differential equations of the form

where the sources on the right-hand side depend on the functions at one lower order. The structure of these sources is such that the
