(5.4)

In the following, we will describe in detail how to find these solutions at leading and first subleading order.

Leading order

At leading order, equation (
5.1
) simplifies to

{\rm d}\psi^{({\color[rgb]{0.8398,0.1523,0.1563}{\pm}}{\color[rgb]{0.1211,0.4648,0.707}{\pm}})}_{0}-\Big[\alpha_{1}\,{\rm d}\log(X_{1}\,{\color[rgb]{0.8398,0.1523,0.1563}{\pm}}\,Y)+\alpha_{2}\,{\rm d}\log(X_{2}\,{\color[rgb]{0.1211,0.4648,0.707}{\pm}}\,Y)\Big]\,\psi^{({\color[rgb]{0.8398,0.1523,0.1563}{\pm}}{\color[rgb]{0.1211,0.4648,0.707}{\pm}})}_{0}+\frac{{\color[rgb]{0.8398,0.1523,0.1563}{\pm}}1{\color[rgb]{0.1211,0.4648,0.707}{\mp}}1}{2}{\rm d}\log\left(\frac{X_{1}\,{\color[rgb]{0.8398,0.1523,0.1563}{\pm}}\,Y}{X_{2}\,{\color[rgb]{0.1211,0.4648,0.707}{\pm}}\,Y}\right)J^{(c)}=0\,.

(5.5)

These equations separate into two qualitatively different cases.

•

The functions
\psi_{0}^{(++)}
and
\psi_{0}^{(--)}
satisfy homogeneous equations

\displaystyle{\rm d}\psi_{0}^{(++)}-\Big[\alpha_{1}\,{\rm d}\log(X_{1}+Y)+\alpha_{2}\,{\rm d}\log(X_{2}+Y)\Big]\psi_{0}^{(++)}

\displaystyle=0\,,

(5.6)

\displaystyle{\rm d}\psi_{0}^{(--)}-\Big[\alpha_{1}\,{\rm d}\log(X_{1}-Y)+\alpha_{2}\,{\rm d}\log(X_{2}-Y)\Big]\psi_{0}^{(--)}

\displaystyle=0\,,

(5.7)

which have the following power-law solutions

\displaystyle\psi_{0}^{(++)}=\,c_{++}(X_{1}+Y)^{\alpha_{1}}(X_{2}+Y)^{\alpha_{2}}\,,

(5.8)

\displaystyle\psi_{0}^{(--)}=\,c_{--}(X_{1}-Y)^{\alpha_{1}}(X_{2}-Y)^{\alpha_{2}}\,,

(5.9)

where the normalizations are arbitrary. In fact, since
\psi_{0}^{(--)}
has unphysical singularities at
X_{i}-Y=0
, we will set its overall coefficient to zero. The solution
\psi_{0}^{(++)}
is degenerate with the disconnected solution, which we discuss below. It is also straightforward to check from (
4.7
) that the integrals that compute these contributions vanish in the
\xi\to 0
limit.

•

The functions
\psi^{(+-)}_{0}
and
\psi^{(-+)}_{0}
satisfy inhomogeneous equations

\displaystyle{\rm d}\psi_{0}^{(+-)}-\Big[\alpha_{1}\,{\rm d}\log(X_{1}+Y)+\alpha_{2}\,{\rm d}\log(X_{2}-Y)\Big]\psi_{0}^{(+-)}

\displaystyle={\rm d}\log\left(\frac{X_{2}-Y}{X_{1}+Y}\right)\hskip 1.0ptJ^{(c)}\,,

(5.10)

\displaystyle{\rm d}\psi_{0}^{(-+)}-\Big[\alpha_{1}\,{\rm d}\log(X_{1}-Y)+\alpha_{2}\,{\rm d}\log(X_{2}+Y)\Big]\psi_{0}^{(-+)}

\displaystyle={\rm d}\log\left(\frac{X_{1}-Y}{X_{2}+Y}\right)\hskip 1.0ptJ^{(c)}\,,

(5.11)

where
J^{(c)}
is given by (
3.42
).
Imposing regularity as
X_{1}\to Y
and
X_{2}\to Y
, we find

\psi_{0}^{(+-)}(X_{1},X_{2},Y)=-c_{\hskip-1.22911pt\raisebox{-2.2604pt}{\includegraphics[scale]{Figures/Equations/Collapsed.pdf}}}\,\frac{1}{\alpha_{2}}\frac{(X_{1}+X_{2})^{1+\alpha_{1}+\alpha_{2}}}{X_{1}+Y}\,{}_{2}F_{1}\bigg[\begin{array}[]{c}1\ ,\ 1+\alpha_{1}\\
1-\alpha_{2}\end{array}\bigg\rvert-\frac{X_{2}-Y}{X_{1}+Y}\,\bigg]\,.

(5.12)

The function
\psi_{0}^{(-+)}
takes the same form, with
\alpha_{1}\leftrightarrow\alpha_{2}
and
X_{1}\leftrightarrow X_{2}
. Using hypergeometric identities, it can be verified that the sum
\psi_{0}^{(+-)}+\psi_{0}^{(-+)}
reproduces the solution obtained in
[
8
]
.

In addition to these connected solutions, we require the disconnected contribution, which is given by a product of the contact solutions (
3.17
) for each of the two vertices. In the limit
\xi\to 0
, the leading disconnected solution is

\psi^{(\raisebox{1.25pt}{\resizebox{753480}{}{\hskip-1.59442pt\raisebox{0.3014pt}{\resizebox{1356540}{}{
\hbox to28.85pt{\vbox to3.25pt{\pgfpicture\makeatletter\hbox{\hskip 1.62263pt\lower-1.62263pt\hbox to0.0pt{\lxSVG@begingroup@{_scopebegin} \lxSVG@begingroup@{stroke} \lxSVG@begingroup@{fill} \lxSVG@setlinewidth{\the\pgflinewidth}\lxSVG@begingroup@{stroke-width} \lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\nullfont\hbox to0.0pt{\lxSVG@begingroup@{_scopebegin} {{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces}}
{}{{}}{}{{{}}{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces}{}{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces}{}{}{}{}{}}{}\lxSVG@fillstroke\lxSVG@drawpath@unclipped{M 0 0 M 1.97 0 C 1.97 1.09 1.09 1.97 0 1.97 C -1.09 1.97 -1.97 1.09 -1.97 0 C -1.97 -1.09 -1.09 -1.97 0 -1.97 C 1.09 -1.97 1.97 -1.09 1.97 0 Z M 0 0}{} \lx@inpgf@ignorespaces
{}{{}}{}{{{}}{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces}{}{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces}{}{}{}{}{}}{}\lxSVG@fillstroke\lxSVG@drawpath@unclipped{M 35.43 0 M 37.4 0 C 37.4 1.09 36.52 1.97 35.43 1.97 C 34.35 1.97 33.46 1.09 33.46 0 C 33.46 -1.09 34.35 -1.97 35.43 -1.97 C 36.52 -1.97 37.4 -1.09 37.4 0 Z M 35.43 0}{} \lx@inpgf@ignorespaces
{}{{}}{}
{}{}\lxSVG@begingroup@{_scopebegin} \lxSVG@setlinewidth{\the\pgflinewidth}\lxSVG@begingroup@{stroke-width} \lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\lxSVG@setdash{2.5pt,1.75pt}{0.0pt}\lxSVG@begingroup@{stroke-dasharray,stroke-dashoffset} \lx@inpgf@ignorespaces{}\lxSVG@stroke\lxSVG@drawpath@unclipped{M 1.38 0 L 35.43 0}{fill:none} \lx@inpgf@ignorespaces
\lxSVG@closescope
\lxSVG@closescope {{
{}{}{}{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces}{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces}}}{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces}{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces}\hss}\lxSVG@discardpath\lxSVG@closescope \hss}}\lxSVG@closescope\endpgfpicture}}}}}})}_{0}=-2c_{\hskip-1.22911pt\raisebox{-2.2604pt}{\includegraphics[scale]{Figures/Equations/Collapsed.pdf}}}(X_{1}+Y)^{\alpha_{1}}(X_{2}+Y)^{\alpha_{2}}\,,

(5.13)

which happens to take the same functional form as (
5.8
).
It is convenient to normalize the disconnected contribution by
c_{\hskip-1.22911pt\raisebox{-2.2604pt}{\includegraphics[scale]{Figures/Equations/Collapsed.pdf}}}
. This choice is useful for two reasons: first,
c_{\hskip-1.22911pt\raisebox{-2.2604pt}{\includegraphics[scale]{Figures/Equations/Collapsed.pdf}}}
depends on
\alpha_{1}
and
\alpha_{2}
, which simplifies taking the limit in which these parameters are scaled to zero; second, it allows us to keep track of how the solution depends on the normalization of
J^{(c)}
.

By combining (
5.12
) and (
5.13
), we obtain the wavefunction for a single massive exchange with generic parameters
\alpha_{1}
and
\alpha_{2}
.
Since we are interested in the four-point function, we want to take the limit
\alpha\equiv\alpha_{1}=\alpha_{2}\to 0
. However, this limit has to be taken with care, since the individual components of the wavefunction are actually singular in this limit. In fact, requiring this limit to be regular fixes the relative normalization between the connected and disconnected components. Putting these pieces together, we obtain

\boxed{\psi_{0}=\psi_{0}^{(+-)}+\psi_{0}^{(-+)}-\left(\frac{1}{\alpha}+\frac{\pi^{2}}{6}\alpha\right)\psi^{(\raisebox{1.25pt}{\resizebox{753480}{}{\hskip-1.59442pt\raisebox{0.3014pt}{\resizebox{1356540}{}{

which is finite in the limit

. Substituting the limiting forms of (

Note that

in this limit, so that

is finite.

\psi_{0}=-2c_{\hskip-1.22911pt\raisebox{-2.2604pt}{\includegraphics[scale]{Figures/Equations/Collapsed.pdf}}}\alpha\left[{\rm Li}_{2}\left(-\frac{X_{1}-Y}{X_{2}+Y}\right)+{\rm Li}_{2}\left(-\frac{X_{2}-Y}{X_{1}+Y}\right)+\frac{1}{2}\log^{2}\left(\frac{X_{1}+Y}{X_{2}+Y}\right)-\,\frac{\pi^{2}}{6}\right].

(5.15)

The linear combination (
5.14
) involves

and
1/\alpha
divergences, but these cancel, so that
\psi_{0}
is finite in the limit
\alpha\to 0
, and the final result has transcendentality two. The
\pi^{2}/6
term ensures that
\psi_{0}
vanishes in the soft limit
Y\to 0
, as required by the original time integral.

Polylogs and symbols

We have seen that, at leading order, the differential equations can be solved for arbitrary values of
\alpha
. At subleading order, however, this is generally not possible. For simplicity, we therefore expand around
\alpha=0
. The various contributions to the wavefunction can then be expressed in terms of (generalized)
polylogarithms
.

Functions of the type that will appear can be written as iterated integrals

F^{(n)}=\int{\rm d}\log R_{1}\circ\dots\circ{\rm d}\log R_{n}=\int_{a}^{b}\left(\int_{a}^{t}{\rm d}\log R_{1}\circ\dots\circ{\rm d}\log R_{n-1}\right){\rm d}\log R_{n}(t)\,,

(5.16)

where
n
is the transcendentality,
R_{i}
are rational functions, and
a
and
b
are rational numbers. The second equality implicitly defines the composition
\circ
of the iterated integrals as in
[
37
]
. Much of the important information about the function
F^{(n)}
, including the locations of its branch points and its differential, can be reconstructed from the rational factors
R_{i}
.
A convenient way to capture this information is through the so-called
symbol

[
38
,
39
,
37
]
. (See
[
29
,
30
]
for a review, and
[
5
,
42
,
2
]
for related applications in the cosmological context.)

The symbol is essentially a simple way to keep track of the factors in the iterated integral (
5.16
) and their ordering. Concretely, the symbol of (
5.16
) is

\mathcal{S}(F^{(n)})=R_{1}\otimes\cdots\otimes R_{n}\,,

(5.17)

where
\otimes
denotes the tensor product taken in the multiplicative group of rational functions.
Terms separated by

\otimes
should implicitly be thought of as being arguments of a logarithm, so that
\otimes
has the same multilinearity properties as products of logarithms.
The leftmost entries of the symbol encode the branch points of the corresponding function. The discontinuities across these branch cuts are obtained by deleting the entry corresponding to the branch point. The resulting symbol is the symbol of the discontinuity. Similarly, the symbol also has information about the differential of the corresponding function. In this case, one reads from right to left. Concretely, we produce the differential of a symbol by replacing the last entries by
{\rm d}\log
of their arguments.

In the end, the symbol encodes most of the information about polylogarithmic functions, but with a much more economical presentation.
As an example, the symbol of (
5.15
) is

{\cal S}(\psi_{0})=\frac{X_{1}+Y}{X_{1}+X_{2}}\otimes\frac{X_{2}-Y}{X_{2}+Y}+\frac{X_{2}+Y}{X_{1}+X_{2}}\otimes\frac{X_{1}-Y}{X_{1}+Y}\,.

(5.18)

The symbol does project out some of the information present in the original function; in particular, terms of lower transcendentality times zeta values are lost (for example, the constant
\pi^{2}/6
in (
5.15
) is absent in the symbol).
In most cases of interest, it is possible to integrate the symbol to recover the full function by imposing appropriate boundary conditions. In the case of (
5.15
), this boundary condition is that the function vanishes as
Y\to 0

[
42
]
.

Subleading order

After this digression on polylogs and symbols, it is now straightforward to continue the analysis at subleading order.
We need to take into account that the lower-order solutions
\psi_{0}^{(+-)}
and
\psi_{0}^{(-+)}
are multiplied by
\xi
in the second line of (
5.1
) and can therefore act as sources for
\psi_{1}^{(\pm\pm)}
. There are again two qualitatively different cases.

•

The functions
\psi_{1}^{(+-)}
and
\psi_{1}^{(-+)}
satisfy homogeneous equations

\displaystyle{\rm d}\psi_{1}^{(+-)}-\Big[\alpha_{1}\,{\rm d}\log(X_{1}+Y)+\alpha_{2}\,{\rm d}\log(X_{2}-Y)\Big]\psi_{1}^{(+-)}

\displaystyle=0\,,

(5.19)

\displaystyle{\rm d}\psi_{1}^{(-+)}-\Big[\alpha_{1}\,{\rm d}\log(X_{1}-Y)+\alpha_{2}\,{\rm d}\log(X_{2}+Y)\Big]\psi_{1}^{(-+)}

\displaystyle=0\,,

(5.20)

which lead to

\displaystyle\psi_{1}^{(+-)}=c_{+-}\,(X_{1}+Y)^{\alpha_{1}}(X_{2}-Y)^{\alpha_{2}}\,,

(5.21)

\displaystyle\psi_{1}^{(-+)}=c_{-+}\,(X_{1}-Y)^{\alpha_{1}}(X_{2}+Y)^{\alpha_{2}}\,,

(5.22)

where
c_{+-}
and
c_{-+}
are integration constants (that eventually will be set to zero).

•

The functions
\psi_{1}^{(++)}
and
\psi_{1}^{(--)}
satisfy inhomogeneous equations

\displaystyle{\rm d}\psi_{1}^{(++)}-\Big[\alpha_{1}\,{\rm d}\log(X_{1}+Y)+\alpha_{2}\,{\rm d}\log(X_{2}+Y)\Big]\psi_{1}^{(++)}

\displaystyle=S^{++}\,,

(5.23)

\displaystyle{\rm d}\psi_{1}^{(--)}-\Big[\alpha_{1}\,{\rm d}\log(X_{1}-Y)+\alpha_{2}\,{\rm d}\log(X_{2}-Y)\Big]\psi_{1}^{(--)}

\displaystyle=S^{--}\,,

(5.24)

where the sources are

S^{\pm\pm}\equiv{\rm d}\log\left(\frac{X_{1}\pm Y}{Y}\right)\,\psi^{(-+)}_{0}+{\rm d}\log\left(\frac{X_{2}\pm Y}{Y}\right)\psi^{(+-)}_{0}\,.

(5.25)

For general
\alpha_{i}
, these source functions are Gauss hypergeometric functions, so one expects the solutions
\psi_{1}^{(\pm\pm)}
to be expressible in terms of generalized hypergeometric functions. However, we have not been able to obtain a closed-form expression in this case. Fortunately, no such formula is required in the limit
\alpha_{i}\to 0
.

We therefore solve the equations (
5.23
) and (
5.24
) perturbatively as
\alpha\equiv\alpha_{i}\to 0
. We first consider
\psi_{1}^{(++)}
. To order
\alpha^{0}
, its solution is

\psi_{1}^{(++)}=\frac{c_{\hskip-1.22911pt\raisebox{-2.2604pt}{\includegraphics[scale]{Figures/Equations/Collapsed.pdf}}}}{\alpha}\,f^{(-2)}+c_{\hskip-1.22911pt\raisebox{-2.2604pt}{\includegraphics[scale]{Figures/Equations/Collapsed.pdf}}}\,f^{(-1)}+c_{\hskip-1.22911pt\raisebox{-2.2604pt}{\includegraphics[scale]{Figures/Equations/Collapsed.pdf}}}\alpha\,f^{(0)}-c_{+}\frac{c_{\hskip-1.22911pt\raisebox{-2.2604pt}{\includegraphics[scale]{Figures/Equations/Collapsed.pdf}}}}{\alpha^{2}}\,,

(5.26)

where the first two coefficient functions are

\displaystyle f^{(-2)}

\displaystyle=\log\left(\frac{4Y^{2}}{X_{1}^{+}X_{2}^{+}}\right)-c_{+}\log(X_{1}^{+}X_{2}^{+})\,,

(5.27)

\displaystyle f^{(-1)}

\displaystyle=\frac{1}{2}\log^{2}\left(\frac{X_{1}^{+}}{X_{2}^{+}}\right)-\log\Big(X_{1}^{+}X_{2}^{+}\Big)\log\left(\frac{X^{+}_{1}X_{2}^{+}}{4Y^{2}}\right)-\frac{1}{2}c_{+}\log^{2}(X_{1}^{+}X_{2}^{+})\,,

with
X_{12}\equiv X_{1}+X_{2}
and
X_{i}^{\pm}\equiv X_{i}\pm Y
. The terms proportional to
c_{+}
in (
5.26
) and (
5.27
) reflect the freedom to add the
homogeneous solution
-c_{+}\hskip 1.0ptc_{\hskip-1.22911pt\raisebox{-2.2604pt}{\includegraphics[scale]{Figures/Equations/Collapsed.pdf}}}(X_{1}^{+}X_{2}^{+})^{\alpha}/\alpha^{2}
, and these terms arise just from expanding this solution in
\alpha
.
Finally, the function
f^{(0)}
is a transcendentality-three combination of polylogs. Its symbol is

\displaystyle{\cal S}(f^{(0)})

\displaystyle=X_{12}\otimes X_{1}^{-}\otimes\frac{(X_{1}^{+})^{2}}{4Y^{2}}+X_{12}\otimes X_{1}^{+}\otimes\frac{4Y^{2}}{(X_{2}^{+})^{2}}+X_{1}^{+}\otimes X_{2}^{-}\otimes\frac{4Y^{2}}{(X_{2}^{+})^{2}}

\displaystyle+X_{1}^{+}\otimes X_{1}^{+}\otimes\frac{4Y^{2}}{X_{1}^{+}(X_{2}^{+})^{3}}+2Y\otimes X_{1}^{+}X_{2}^{+}\otimes X_{1}^{+}X_{2}^{+}+X_{1}^{+}\otimes X_{2}^{+}\otimes\frac{1}{(X_{1}^{+})^{3}(X_{2}^{+})^{3}}

\displaystyle+X_{1}^{+}X_{2}^{+}\otimes 2Y\otimes X_{1}^{+}X_{2}^{+}-\frac{c_{+}}{2}\,X_{1}^{+}X_{2}^{+}\otimes X_{1}^{+}X_{2}^{+}\otimes X_{1}^{+}X_{2}^{+}+(X_{1}\leftrightarrow X_{2})\,,

(5.28)

where
(X_{1}\leftrightarrow X_{2})
indicates we should add the same expression with
X_{1}
and
X_{2}
interchanged everywhere.
The integration constants in the particular solution
in (
5.27
) and (
5.28
) are fixed by two considerations: 1) we fix constants so that the only symbol entries are
X_{12},X_{1}^{\pm},X_{2}^{\pm}
and
2Y
and 2) we impose that the solution at each order in
\alpha
has uniform transcendentality. The solution
f^{(0)}
can be shifted by an arbitrary transcendental constant that does not affect its symbol.
11
11

11

We expect that this constant can be determined by requiring the final solution to vanish as
Y\to 0
.

Similarly,
\psi_{1}^{(--)}
can be written as

\psi_{1}^{(--)}=\frac{c_{\hskip-1.22911pt\raisebox{-2.2604pt}{\includegraphics[scale]{Figures/Equations/Collapsed.pdf}}}}{\alpha}\,g^{(-2)}+c_{\hskip-1.22911pt\raisebox{-2.2604pt}{\includegraphics[scale]{Figures/Equations/Collapsed.pdf}}}\,g^{(-1)}+c_{\hskip-1.22911pt\raisebox{-2.2604pt}{\includegraphics[scale]{Figures/Equations/Collapsed.pdf}}}\alpha\,g^{(0)}+c_{-}\frac{c_{\hskip-1.22911pt\raisebox{-2.2604pt}{\includegraphics[scale]{Figures/Equations/Collapsed.pdf}}}}{\alpha^{2}}\,,

(5.29)

where the first two coefficient functions are

\displaystyle g^{(-2)}

\displaystyle=\log\left(\frac{4Y^{2}}{X_{1}^{-}X_{2}^{-}}\right)+c_{-}\log(X_{1}^{-}X_{2}^{-})

(5.30)

\displaystyle g^{(-1)}

\displaystyle=2\hskip 1.0pt{\rm Li}_{2}\left(-\frac{X_{1}^{-}}{2Y}\right)+2\hskip 1.0pt{\rm Li}_{2}\left(-\frac{X_{2}^{-}}{2Y}\right)+2\log^{2}(2Y)-\frac{1}{2}\left(1-c_{-}\right)\log^{2}(X_{1}^{-}X_{2}^{-})\,,

and the coefficient

.
As before, the function

has transcendentality three and is rather complex, so we just display its symbol

\displaystyle{\cal S}(g^{(0)})

\displaystyle=X_{12}\otimes X_{1}^{-}\otimes\frac{(X_{2}^{-})^{2}}{4Y^{2}}+X_{12}X_{1}^{+}\otimes X_{1}^{+}\otimes\frac{4Y^{2}}{(X_{1}^{-})^{2}}+X_{1}^{+}\otimes X_{1}^{-}\otimes\frac{1}{(X_{1}^{-})^{2}(X_{2}^{-})^{2}}

\displaystyle+X_{1}^{+}\otimes X_{2}^{-}\otimes\frac{4Y^{2}}{(X_{1}^{-})^{2}}+\frac{1}{2}X_{1}^{-}X_{2}^{-}\otimes X_{1}^{-}X_{2}^{-}\otimes\frac{1}{X_{1}^{-}X_{2}^{-}}+X_{1}^{+}X_{2}^{+}\otimes 2Y\otimes X_{1}^{-}X_{2}^{-}

\displaystyle+2Y\otimes X_{1}^{-}X_{2}^{-}\otimes X_{1}^{-}X_{2}^{-}+\frac{1}{2}c_{-}\,X_{1}^{-}X_{2}^{-}\otimes X_{1}^{-}X_{2}^{-}\otimes X_{1}^{-}X_{2}^{-}+(X_{1}\leftrightarrow X_{2})\,.

which can be integrated back into the full function by imposing appropriate boundary conditions.

c_{+}=c_{-}=1
, this is the unique linear combination (up to an additive constant) that remains regular in the
\alpha\to 0
limit, with no folded singularities. We can write the resulting finite wavefunction as

\psi_{1}=c_{\hskip-1.22911pt\raisebox{-2.2604pt}{\includegraphics[scale]{Figures/Equations/Collapsed.pdf}}}\alpha\left(f^{(0)}+g^{(0)}-2h^{(0)}\right)\ ,

(5.37)

where the functions
f^{(0)}
,
g^{(0)}
and
h^{(0)}
are given by (
5.28
), (
5.31
) and (
5.35
), respectively, with
c_{+}=c_{-}=1
. The factor
c_{\hskip-1.22911pt\raisebox{-2.2604pt}{\includegraphics[scale]{Figures/Equations/Collapsed.pdf}}}\alpha
is
-1/2
as
\alpha\to 0
, and we can write the symbol of the resulting first-order wavefunction as

\displaystyle{\cal S}(\psi_{1})

\displaystyle=X_{12}\otimes X_{1}^{-}\otimes\frac{4Y^{2}}{X_{1}^{+}X_{2}^{-}}+X_{12}\otimes X_{1}^{+}\otimes\frac{X_{1}^{-}X_{2}^{+}}{4Y^{2}}+X_{1}^{+}\otimes X_{2}^{-}\otimes\frac{X_{1}^{-}X_{2}^{+}}{4Y^{2}}

(5.38)

\displaystyle+X_{1}^{+}\otimes X_{2}^{+}\otimes\frac{4Y^{2}}{X_{1}^{-}X_{2}^{-}}+2Y\otimes X_{1}^{-}\otimes\frac{X_{2}^{+}}{X_{2}^{-}}+2Y\otimes X_{1}^{+}\otimes\frac{X_{2}^{-}}{X_{2}^{+}}

\displaystyle+X_{1}^{+}\otimes X_{1}^{-}\otimes\frac{X_{2}^{-}}{X_{2}^{+}}+(X_{1}\leftrightarrow X_{2})\,,

which is manifestly free of folded singularities (i.e. no
X_{1}^{-}
or
X_{2}^{-}
in the leftmost slot). We have checked that this matches the symbol of the solution obtained in
[
34
]
.

It is possible to continue this procedure to higher orders in
\xi
. At
O(\xi^{n})
, we would find a solution of transcendentality
n+2
, fixed by the same boundary conditions of regularity as
\alpha\to 0
and absence of folded singularities. It would be interesting to characterize the polylogarithmic functions that appear to all orders.

5.2
Heavy Particle Exchange

It is also interesting to consider the limit where the mass of the exchanged particle goes to infinity, so that
\xi\to\infty
.
In this limit, the structure of the differential equations simplifies substantially and encodes the emergence of the effective field theory (EFT) expansion.

To begin, we write the set of equations in (
5.1
) in the following matrix form

{\rm d}I-(A^{(0)}+\nu\,A^{(1)})\cdot I=J\,,

(5.39)

where we have introduced

I\equiv\left[\begin{array}[]{c}\psi^{(++)}\\
\psi^{(--)}\\
\psi^{(+-)}\\
\psi^{(-+)}\\
\end{array}\right]\,,\hskip 28.45274ptJ\equiv\left[\begin{array}[]{c}0\\
0\\
(\ell_{2}^{+}-\ell_{1}^{-})\hskip 1.0ptJ^{(c)}\\
(\ell_{1}^{+}-\ell_{2}^{-})\hskip 1.0ptJ^{(c)}\\
\end{array}\right]\,,

(5.40)

so that the contact solution
J^{(c)}
, defined by (
3.42
), appears as a source in the equations for
\psi^{(\pm\pm)}
. It is convenient to extract the components proportional to
\nu
, so that
the relevant connection matrices in (
5.39
) are

\displaystyle A^{(0)}

\displaystyle\equiv\begin{bmatrix}\alpha_{1}\hskip 1.0pt\ell_{1}^{+}+\alpha_{2}\hskip 1.0pt\ell_{2}^{+}&0&\frac{1}{2}(\ell_{0}-\ell_{1}^{+})&\frac{1}{2}(\ell_{0}-\ell_{2}^{+})\\[2.0pt]
0&\alpha_{1}\hskip 1.0pt\ell_{1}^{-}+\alpha_{2}\hskip 1.0pt\ell_{2}^{-}&\frac{1}{2}(\ell_{0}-\ell_{2}^{-})&\frac{1}{2}(\ell_{0}-\ell_{1}^{-})\\[2.0pt]
\frac{1}{2}(\ell_{0}-\ell_{1}^{-})&\frac{1}{2}(\ell_{0}-\ell_{2}^{+})&\alpha_{1}\hskip 1.0pt\ell_{1}^{-}+\alpha_{2}\hskip 1.0pt\ell_{2}^{+}&0\\[2.0pt]
\frac{1}{2}(\ell_{0}-\ell_{2}^{-})&\frac{1}{2}(\ell_{0}-\ell_{1}^{+})&0&\alpha_{1}\hskip 1.0pt\ell_{1}^{+}+\alpha_{2}\hskip 1.0pt\ell_{2}^{-}\end{bmatrix},

(5.41)

\displaystyle A^{(1)}

\displaystyle\equiv\begin{bmatrix}0&\quad 0&\quad\ell_{1}^{+}-\ell_{0}&\quad\ell_{2}^{+}-\ell_{0}\\
0&\quad 0&\quad\ell_{2}^{-}-\ell_{0}&\quad\ell_{1}^{-}-\ell_{0}\\
\ell_{1}^{-}-\ell_{0}&\quad\ell_{2}^{+}-\ell_{0}&\quad 0&\quad 0\\
\ell_{2}^{-}-\ell_{0}&\quad\ell_{1}^{+}-\ell_{0}&\quad 0&\quad 0\end{bmatrix},

where as before
\ell_{i}^{\pm}\equiv{\rm d}\log(X_{i}\pm Y)
and
\ell_{0}\equiv{\rm d}\log Y
.
The choice to write the equation directly in terms of
\nu
organizes the large-mass limit in a more convenient way than
\xi
, because this is the parameter that we are scaling to be large in this limit.

Equation (
5.39
) is form-valued, and so actually implies three separate equations. To make this explicit, it is useful to momentarily restore indices to write

{\rm d}Z^{i}\Big(\partial_{Z^{i}}I^{a}-(A_{i}^{(0)}{}^{\hskip 1.0ptab}+\nu\,A_{i}^{(1)}{}^{\hskip 1.0ptab})\,I^{b}\Big)={\rm d}Z^{i}\,J_{i}^{a}\,.

(5.42)

This is separately true for each kinematic differential
{\rm d}Z_{i}=\{{\rm d}X_{1,2},{\rm d}Y\}
, implying three equations. They are not independent, and solving any one of them provides a vector of functions that satisfies them all. For concreteness, we will explicitly solve the
X_{1}
-equation, and then comment on the relation to the other equations.

We want to solve (
5.42
) perturbatively as
\nu\to\infty
.
12
12

12

For unitary dS representations,
\nu
goes to infinity along the imaginary axis. Since we are expanding in
\nu^{-1}
, we are capturing the part of the answer that is complex analytic in this parameter and so this subtlety does not matter. However, it would be very interesting to understand how to capture the nonperturbative contributions in
\nu
from this perspective, which carry the signatures of particle production.

To facilitate this, we expand

I=\sum_{n=0}^{\infty}\nu^{-n}\,I_{n}\,,

(5.43)

and solve for the component functions of the vector
I_{n}
at each order in
\nu
.

Leading order

At leading order, equation (
5.42
) becomes trivial

-\nu\,A^{(1)}\cdot I_{0}=0\,,

(5.44)

and just sets
I_{0}=0
. At order
\nu
, the equation is again algebraic and reads

-\,A^{(1)}_{X_{1}}\cdot I_{1}=J_{X_{1}}\,,

(5.45)

where
A^{(1)}_{X_{1}}
is the
X_{1}
-component (the coefficient of
{\rm d}X_{1}
) of
A^{(1)}
.
By inverting the matrix
A^{(1)}_{X_{1}}
, we obtain the first-order solution

I_{1}=-\big(A_{X_{1}}^{(1)}\big)^{-1}\cdot J_{X_{1}}=\left[\begin{array}[]{c}J^{(c)}\\
-J^{(c)}\\
0\\
0\\
\end{array}\right].

(5.46)

We see that, at this order, the individual solutions for the basis elements are nonzero, but when we sum them to obtain the actual wavefunction, we find that
\psi_{1}=0
. One can readily check that (
5.46
) also solves the
X_{2}
and
Y
-equations.

At next order, we have to solve the equation

\frac{1}{\nu}\bigg((\partial_{X_{1}}-A^{(0)}_{X_{1}})\cdot I_{1}-A^{(1)}_{X_{1}}\cdot I_{2}\bigg)=0\,.

(5.47)

By inverting
A^{(1)}
, this admits an algebraic solution

I_{2}=\big(A^{(1)}_{X_{1}}\big)^{-1}\cdot\big(\partial_{X_{1}}-A^{(0)}_{X_{1}}\big)\cdot I_{1}\,.

(5.48)

Upon substituting in the explicit expressions, we find

I_{2}=\left[\begin{array}[]{r}\frac{1}{2}J^{(c)}\\
-\frac{1}{2}J^{(c)}\\
D_{X_{1}}^{+}J^{(c)}\\
-D_{X_{1}}^{-}J^{(c)}\\
\end{array}\right],

(5.49)

where, for future convenience, we have defined the following two differential operators

D_{X_{1}}^{\pm}=(X_{1}\pm Y)\partial_{X_{1}}-\alpha_{1}\,.

(5.50)

When we sum the entries of
I_{2}
, we get

\boxed{\psi_{2}=2Y\partial_{X_{1}}J^{(c)}}\ ,

(5.51)

which is nonzero (unlike
\psi_{1}
).

Our case of interest is the four-point function of conformal scalars arising from exchanging a massive particle. We should therefore evaluate (
3.42
) and (
5.51
) as
\alpha_{1},\alpha_{2}\to 0
. Taking this limit, we find

\psi_{2}=-\frac{2Y}{X_{1}+X_{2}}\,.

(5.52)

Notice that this wavefunction only has the total energy singularity of a contact interaction, and indeed is precisely the four-point function of conformally coupled scalars with a
\phi^{4}
interaction. Physically, this is a satisfying result: in the infinite-mass limit, the exchange of a massive particle reduces to an effective point-like contact interaction.

Subleading order

It is interesting to continue to solve (
5.39
) iteratively at subleading order. As we will see, this reproduces the EFT expansion from integrating out the massive particle. First, we note that the recursive structure of (
5.47
) persists at each order

\frac{1}{\nu^{n}}\bigg((\partial_{X_{1}}-A^{(0)}_{X_{1}})\cdot I_{n}-A^{(1)}_{X_{1}}\cdot I_{n+1}\bigg)=0\,,

(5.53)

so that a formal solution is

I_{n+1}=\big(A^{(1)}_{X_{1}}\big)^{-1}\cdot\big(\partial_{X_{1}}-A^{(0)}_{X_{1}}\big)\cdot I_{n}\,.

(5.54)

This equation can be written in a suggestive way by introducing the matrix

M_{X_{1}}\equiv\big(A^{(1)}_{X_{1}}\big)^{-1}\cdot\big(\partial_{X_{1}}-A^{(0)}_{X_{1}}\big)=\left[\begin{array}[]{cccc}\tfrac{1}{2}&0&D_{X_{1}}^{-}&0\\
0&\tfrac{1}{2}&0&D_{X_{1}}^{+}\\
D_{X_{1}}^{+}&0&\tfrac{1}{2}&0\\
0&D_{X_{1}}^{-}&0&\tfrac{1}{2}\end{array}\right],

(5.55)

so that
I_{n}=M_{X_{1}}^{n-1}\cdot I_{1}
.
It is convenient at this point to consider separately the cases where
n
is even or odd. To do this, we notice that the action of
M^{2}_{X_{1}}
on a general vector is relatively simple:

M_{X_{1}}^{2}.\left[\begin{array}[]{c}F_{1}\\
F_{2}\\
F_{3}\\
F_{4}\end{array}\right]=\left[\begin{array}[]{c}({\cal C}_{X_{1}}-D_{X_{1}}^{+})F_{1}+D_{X_{1}}^{-}F_{3}\\
({\cal C}_{X_{1}}-D_{X_{1}}^{-})F_{2}+D_{X_{1}}^{+}F_{4}\\
({\cal C}_{X_{1}}-D_{X_{1}}^{-})F_{3}+D_{X_{1}}^{+}F_{1}\\
({\cal C}_{X_{1}}-D_{X_{1}}^{+})F_{4}+D_{X_{1}}^{-}F_{2}\\
\end{array}\right],

(5.56)

where we have defined the second-order differential operator

\displaystyle{\cal C}_{X_{1}}

\displaystyle=D_{X_{1}}^{\pm}D_{X_{1}}^{\mp}+D_{X_{1}}^{\mp}+\frac{1}{4}

(5.57)

\displaystyle=(X_{1}^{2}-Y^{2})\partial_{X_{1}}^{2}+2(1-\alpha_{1})X_{1}\partial_{X_{1}}+\left(\alpha_{1}-\frac{1}{2}\right)^{2}\,.

Adding up the various components, we find the extremely simple recursion relation between wavefunctions at different orders in
\nu
:

\psi_{n+2}={\cal C}_{X_{1}}\psi_{n}\,.

(5.58)

Since
\psi_{1}=0
, we find that the odd contributions vanish,
\psi_{2n+1}=0
, while the even contributions are given by
\psi_{2n}={\cal C}_{X_{1}}^{n-1}\psi_{2}
. Putting this all together, we find that the wavefunction in the large mass limit is

\boxed{\psi_{\rm EFT}=\sum_{n=1}^{\infty}\nu^{-2n}\,{\cal C}_{X_{1}}^{n-1}\left(2Y\partial_{X_{1}}J^{(c)}\right)}\ .

(5.59)

Notice that we have written
\psi_{\rm EFT}
in terms of the differential operator
{\cal C}_{X_{1}}
. One can easily check that the four-point function (
5.52
) satisfies
({\cal C}_{X_{1}}-{\cal C}_{X_{2}})\psi_{2}=0
, so we could have just as well written the answer in terms of
X_{2}
(and indeed this is the expression we would have obtained by solving the
X_{2}
-equations). Alternatively, we can straightforwardly check that these expressions solve the
X_{2}
and
Y
-equations as well. It is worth noting that the nontrivial compatibility between these equations relies on the fact that
\psi
satisfies
({\cal C}_{X_{1}}-{\cal C}_{X_{2}})\psi=0
, which is equivalent to the conformal Ward identities arising from de Sitter symmetry
[
4
]
. It is rather interesting that these Ward identities are an emergent consequence of the first-order system (
5.39
).

The expression (
5.59
) is a remarkably compact formula for the all-orders EFT expansion in the large
\nu
limit. We see that, in this limit, the differential equations rather nicely organize themselves into algebraic equations that can be solved iteratively. It is further interesting to note that (
5.59
) can be formally summed to obtain

\psi_{\rm EFT}=-\frac{1}{{\cal C}_{X_{1}}-\nu^{2}}\,\psi_{2}\,,

(5.60)

where

\psi_{2}
is the contact solution (
5.52
). By acting with the differential operator
{\cal C}_{X_{1}}-\nu^{2}
on both sides, we obtain a second-order equation satisfied by the
full
wavefunction. (To compare this with
[
4
]
, note that
{\cal C}_{X_{1}}\equiv\Delta_{u}+\frac{1}{4}
, where
\Delta_{u}
is the differential operator introduced in
[
4
]
.)
We can think of the EFT solution as formally inverting this differential operator, which removes the zero mode that contains the nonperturbative in
\nu^{-1}
pieces due to cosmological particle production in de Sitter.
This is reflected in the fact that the series (
5.59
) is only asymptotic in
\nu^{-1}
(see also
[
28
]
). It would be very interesting to understand whether these nonperturbative corrections can be deduced from the series (
5.59
) using techniques from resurgence.

5.3
Collapsed Limit

It is instructive to analyze the first-order system in a special kinematic regime. In this subsection, we study the collapsed limit

Y\to 0
and show that the system can be solved exactly for arbitrary mass. This makes the emergence of particle production particularly transparent.

It is most convenient to start from the equations (
3.46
):

), and we have restored the coupling
g^{2}
for clarity.
In order to simplify the system, it is helpful to define

\displaystyle\hat{\psi}

\displaystyle\equiv\frac{1}{2Y}\hskip 1.0pt\psi\,,

(5.62)

\displaystyle\hat{G}

\displaystyle\equiv\frac{1}{2Y}\left[(\alpha_{1}-\xi)\hskip 1.0ptY\hskip 1.0pt\tilde{\psi}+2Y\hskip 1.0ptg^{2}\hskip 1.0ptc_{\hskip-1.22911pt\raisebox{-2.2604pt}{\includegraphics[scale]{Figures/Equations/Collapsed.pdf}}}\hskip 1.0pt(X_{1}+X_{2})^{\alpha_{1}+\alpha_{2}}\right],

so that (
5.61
) becomes

\displaystyle\partial_{X_{1}}\hat{\psi}

\displaystyle=\frac{1}{X_{1}^{2}-Y^{2}}\Big[(\alpha_{1}+\xi)X_{1}\hat{\psi}-\hat{G}\Big],

(5.63)

\displaystyle\partial_{X_{1}}\hat{G}

\displaystyle=\frac{(\alpha_{1}-\xi)}{X_{1}^{2}-Y^{2}}\Big[X_{1}\hat{G}-(\alpha_{1}-\xi)Y^{2}\hat{\psi}\Big]+g^{2}\hskip 1.0ptc_{\hskip-1.22911pt\raisebox{-2.2604pt}{\includegraphics[scale]{Figures/Equations/Collapsed.pdf}}}(\alpha_{1}+\alpha_{2})(X_{1}+X_{2})^{\alpha_{1}+\alpha_{2}-1}.

Taking the limits
\alpha_{1},\alpha_{2}\to 0
and
Y\to 0
,
we then obtain the reduced system

\displaystyle\partial_{X_{1}}\hat{\psi}

\displaystyle=\frac{\xi}{X_{1}}\hat{\psi}-\frac{1}{X_{1}^{2}}\hat{G}\,,

(5.64)

\displaystyle\partial_{X_{1}}\hat{G}

\displaystyle=-\frac{\xi}{X_{1}}\hat{G}-\frac{g^{2}}{X_{1}+X_{2}}\,,

where we used
c_{\hskip-1.22911pt\raisebox{-2.2604pt}{\includegraphics[scale]{Figures/Equations/Collapsed.pdf}}}\to-(\alpha_{1}+\alpha_{2})^{-1}
.
We see that the
Y\to 0
limit greatly reduces the complexity of the system. In particular,
\hat{\psi}
has dropped out of the equation for
\hat{G}
, so the system is now in upper-triangular form:
\hat{G}
obeys a sourced homogeneous equation and is determined independently, and then
\hat{\psi}
follows by a single integration.

The only remaining dimensionless kinematic variable in the limit
Y=0
is the ratio
r\equiv X_{2}/X_{1}
, and so it is convenient to express
\hat{\psi}
and
\hat{G}
as

\displaystyle\hat{\psi}(X_{1},X_{2})

\displaystyle=(X_{1}X_{2})^{-1/2}\,\uppsi(r)\,,

(5.65)

\displaystyle\hat{G}(X_{1},X_{2})

\displaystyle=\left(\frac{X_{2}}{X_{1}}\right)^{-1/2}\,{\cal G}(r)\,.

Defining
r\equiv e^{\rho}
, the equations (
5.64
) then take the form

\displaystyle\big(\partial_{\rho}+\nu\big)\uppsi(\rho)

\displaystyle={\cal G}(\rho)\,,

(5.66)

\displaystyle\big(\partial_{\rho}-\nu\big){\cal G}(\rho)

\displaystyle=\frac{g^{2}}{2}{\rm sech}\Big(\frac{\rho}{2}\Big)\,,

where recall
\nu=\xi+\frac{1}{2}
.
For generic
\nu
, the solutions of the first-order system (
5.66
) can be written in terms of exponential and Gauss hypergeometric functions

\displaystyle{\cal G}(\rho)

\displaystyle=2\nu\,A\,e^{\nu\rho}+g^{2}\,F_{-}(\rho)\,,

(5.67)

\displaystyle\hskip-56.9055pt\uppsi(\rho)

\displaystyle=Ae^{\nu\rho}+Be^{-\nu\rho}+\frac{g^{2}}{2\nu}\Big[F_{-}(\rho)-F_{+}(\rho)\Big]\,,

where
A
and
B
are integration constants and

F_{\pm}(\rho)\equiv\frac{e^{\rho/2}}{\frac{1}{2}\pm\nu}\,{}_{2}F_{1}\bigg[\begin{array}[]{c}1\,,\,\tfrac{1}{2}\pm\nu\\[-1.0pt]
\tfrac{3}{2}\pm\nu\end{array}\bigg\rvert-e^{\rho}\,\bigg]\,.

(5.68)

In order to interpret this solution, it is useful to notice that the equations (
5.66
) can be combined into

\boxed{\Big(\partial_{\rho}^{2}-\nu^{2}\Big)\uppsi=\frac{g^{2}}{2}{\rm sech}\left(\frac{\rho}{2}\right)}\ .

(5.69)

For heavy fields, where
\nu=i\mu
(with
\mu\in\mathbb{R}
), this is the equation of a
forced harmonic oscillator
in the kinematic variable
\rho=\log(X_{2}/X_{1})

[
4
]
.
This makes manifest that the solution will display the characteristic oscillations of a massive field.
Here, we have seen this oscillator solution emerge from the first-order system.

6
Conclusions

Adding mass to scalar particles in flat space is a relatively mild modification to the structure of the theory, where the mode functions and (tree-level) analytic structure of observables do not change.
In contrast, massive particles in de Sitter space are substantially different from massless ones.
Perhaps the most relevant feature is that the mode functions become Hankel functions, which leads to a significantly more intricate analytic structure of the associated correlation functions.

In this paper, we have shown that despite this apparent complexity, the differential equations satisfied by massive correlators are governed by remarkably simple combinatorial structures that are very similar to their conformally coupled counterparts.
As in the conformal case, the differential equations can be viewed as a flow through the space of kinematic variables, visualized in terms of graphical tubings and governed by simple rules. There are also interesting new features in the massive case:
1) Massive propagators require additional basis functions, corresponding to new graph tubings, and 2) Tubes pierced by massive propagators can shrink to produce new source functions (while in the conformally coupled case they only grow).
Accounting for these effects, the kinematic flow rules generate the differential equations for arbitrary Feynman graphs.

There are many phenomenologically important questions in which integrals of this type arise. For example, characterizing the signatures of massive particles during inflation requires understanding processes involving massive exchanges
[
23
,
11
,
48
,
6
,
44
,
4
,
7
,
52
,
54
,
17
,
50
,
43
]
. To demonstrate the utility of these techniques, we solved the simplest such case (involving a single massive exchange) in the parametric limits of large and small masses, which are particularly easy to take at the level of the differential equations. The large-mass limit is closely connected to the effective field theory expansion in de Sitter space, and it would be interesting to understand the non-perturbative corrections that arise from cosmological particle production. Furthermore, in Appendix
A
, we describe a dictionary between the equations for massive fields in de Sitter space and massless fields in a power-law cosmology. The small-mass limit is mapped to the de Sitter limit, so a systematic study of this limit may shed some light on the infrared structure of massless fields in de Sitter space, where the deviation from de Sitter serves as a physical regulator.

Finally, it is conceptually interesting that massive correlators share so many similarities with their simpler conformally coupled cousins. Aside from the existence of a kinematic flow, the massive wavefunction can be written as a twisted integral of a universal rational integrand (see Appendix
B
). This is therefore an ideal representation to study the properties of generic Feynman graphs (including features like the Passarino–Veltman reduction and the evaluation of loop momentum integrals). Studying the properties of the
integrand
will also be interesting.
In the conformal case, the integrand is closely related to “cosmological polytopes”
[
5
]
. In the massive setting, this suggests the existence of corresponding “massive cosmological polytopes”, which represent new geometric structures worthy of further exploration.
Relatedly, we saw in several places the emergence of second-order conformal Ward identities from the first-order system of differential equations. From the bulk perspective, these Ward identities follow from the symmetries of de Sitter space. Clarifying how this spacetime picture emerges from the combinatorial structure of the first-order system may therefore illuminate the broader question of how spacetime itself emerges from more fundamental principles.

Appendix A
Massless Integrals

In the main text, we focused on massive fields in exact de Sitter spacetime.
However, all of our formulas also apply to correlation functions of massless scalar fields in a power-law cosmology, after a simple relabeling of parameters. In this appendix, we provide a dictionary between these two situations. (See also
[
16
]
.)

A.1
Power-Law Cosmology

We begin by considering the following action of a massive scalar field in a
(d+1)
-dimensional curved spacetime

S=\int{\rm d}^{d+1}x\sqrt{-g}\Bigg(\frac{1}{2}\phi\left[\square-\frac{d-1}{8d}R\right]\phi-\frac{m^{2}}{2}\phi^{2}+\frac{\kappa}{2}R\phi^{2}-\sum_{p=3}^{\infty}\frac{\lambda_{p}}{p!}\phi^{p}\Bigg)\,,

(A.1)

where we allowed for a coupling to the Ricci scalar
R
, with

\kappa=\begin{cases}\ \ \,0&\text{conformal coupling}\,,\\[6.0pt]
{\displaystyle\frac{d-1}{4d}}&\text{minimal coupling}\,.\end{cases}

(A.2)

We assume that the cosmological background is described by a flat Robertson–Walker metric, with scale factor
a(\eta)
and conformal Hubble parameter
{\cal H}\equiv a^{\prime}/a
. By a Weyl rescaling,
g_{\mu\nu}=a^{2}\eta_{\mu\nu}
and

\phi=a^{-(d-1)/2}\varphi
, the theory can then be cast
as a time-dependent theory in flat Minkowski space:

S=\int{\rm d}^{d+1}x\,\Bigg(-\frac{1}{2}\eta^{\mu\nu}\partial_{\mu}\varphi\partial_{\nu}\varphi-\frac{m^{2}(\eta)}{2}\varphi^{2}-\sum_{p=3}^{\infty}\frac{\lambda_{p}(\eta)}{p!}\varphi^{p}\Bigg)\,,

(A.3)

where the time-dependent mass and couplings are

\displaystyle m^{2}(\eta)

\displaystyle=m^{2}a^{2}-2d\hskip 1.0pt\kappa\bigg({\cal H}^{\prime}+\frac{d-1}{2}{\cal H}^{2}\bigg)\,,

(A.4)

\displaystyle\lambda_{p}(\eta)

\displaystyle=\lambda_{p}\hskip 1.0pta^{2+\frac{1}{2}(d-1)(2-p)}\,.

Note that for
d=3
, the coupling becomes
\lambda_{p}(\eta)=\lambda_{p}\hskip 1.0pta^{4-p}
, which is time-independent for the conformal value
p=4
.

We let the cosmological background be a power law in conformal time:

a(\eta)=\left(\frac{\eta}{\eta_{0}}\right)^{-(1+\varepsilon)}\,.

(A.5)

For
\varepsilon>-1
, the evolution corresponds to
accelerated expansion, while, for
\varepsilon<-1
, we have decelerated collapse. Several cosmologies can be described by this power-law ansatz:
\varepsilon=0
(de Sitter),
\varepsilon=-1
(Minkowski),
\varepsilon=-2
(radiation-dominated) and
\varepsilon=-3
(matter-dominated).

The linear equation of motion for the field (in Fourier space) then is

\varphi_{k}^{\prime\prime}+\Big(k^{2}+m^{2}(\eta)\Big)\varphi_{k}=0\,,

(A.6)

where the effective mass is

m^{2}(\eta)=m^{2}\left(\frac{\eta}{\eta_{0}}\right)^{-2(1+\varepsilon)}-\frac{\kappa\,(1+\varepsilon)}{\eta^{2}}\Bigg(\frac{4d+2d(d-1)(1+\varepsilon)}{2}\Bigg)\,.

(A.7)

Equations of the form (
A.6
) can be solved in terms of Bessel functions if the mass scales like
\eta^{-2}
. In these cases, we can define
m^{2}(\eta)\equiv\mu^{2}(\varepsilon,m)\hskip 1.0pt\eta^{-2}
, so that the Bunch–Davies solution is

\hat{f}_{k}(\eta)=\frac{\sqrt{\pi}}{2}e^{-i\frac{\pi\nu}{2}}(-\eta)^{1/2}H_{\nu}^{(2)}(-k\eta)\,,\qquad\nu\equiv\sqrt{\frac{1}{4}-\mu^{2}(\varepsilon,m)}\,,

(A.8)

where
H_{\nu}^{(2)}
is a Hankel function of the second kind.
Looking at (
A.7
), we see that there are two scenarios with this time dependence for the mass
[
16
]
.

•

\varepsilon=0
: This is the case of a scalar field of generic mass in an exact de Sitter spacetime, which we considered in the main text. It is convenient to define
\eta_{0}\equiv-H^{-1}
. We then have

\nu=\begin{cases}{\displaystyle\sqrt{\frac{1}{4}-\frac{m^{2}}{H^{2}}}}&\text{conformal coupling}\,,\\[12.0pt]
{\displaystyle\sqrt{\frac{d^{2}}{4}-\frac{m^{2}}{H^{2}}}}&\text{minimal coupling}\,.\end{cases}

(A.9)

Note that, for the conformal coupling, the mass is shifted, so that the formula for
\nu
is independent of the spacetime dimension.

•

m=0
: This is the case of a massless field in an arbitrary power-law cosmology (
\varepsilon\neq 0
).
Note that the scaling
m^{2}(\eta)\propto\eta^{-2}
follows for any value of the non-minimal coupling parameter
\kappa
. For the conformal and minimal couplings, the parameter
\nu
simplifies to

\nu=\begin{cases}{\displaystyle\frac{1}{2}}&\text{conformal coupling}\,,\\[12.0pt]
{\displaystyle\frac{1}{2}+\frac{d-1}{2}(1+\varepsilon)}&\text{minimal coupling}\,.\end{cases}

(A.10)

The conformally coupled case was considered in detail in
[
5
,
2
,
3
,
8
,
25
,
31
,
41
,
26
,
35
,
19
,
46
,
33
]
.
Here, we focus on the minimally coupled case.

Given that the mode functions in each of these cases can be written in terms of Hankel functions, we can now relate them to the constructions in the main text.

A.2
Massless Fields

We now describe how the differential equations derived in the main text can be applied to the case of massless fields in a general power-law cosmology. It is useful to briefly summarize the massive construction first.

Recall that in Section
2
, we worked in terms of the original field
\phi
and not the Weyl-transformed field
\varphi=a^{(d-1)/2}\phi
. The mode function for the field
\phi
is then (
2.5
), with vertex factors
V_{i}=i\lambda_{p_{i}}(-H\eta)^{-(d+1)}
, for each vertex
i
.
In order to simplify the structure of the differential equations, we then defined
g_{k}
in (
2.14
) by extracting an overall factor as

f_{k}(\eta)=(-\eta)^{d/2-\nu}\times iH^{\frac{1}{2}(d-1)}\hskip 1.0pte^{-i\frac{\pi\nu}{2}}\frac{g_{k}(\eta)}{\sqrt{2k}}\,.

(A.11)

Since this overall factor involves powers of
\eta
, we absorbed these factors into an effective vertex factor

V_{i,\rm eff}\equiv i\lambda_{p_{i}}H^{-(d+1)}(-\eta)^{-(1+\alpha_{i}+\xi_{i})}\,,

(A.12)

where the parameters
\alpha_{i}
and
\xi_{i}
were defined in (
2.18
). In Section
3
, we then derived differential equations satisfied by the wavefunction in terms of these parameters.

We now consider the analogous construction for a massless field. In that case, the mode function of
\phi
is

\displaystyle f_{k}(\eta)

\displaystyle=i\eta_{0}^{-\frac{1}{2}(d-1)(1+\varepsilon)}e^{-i\frac{\pi\nu}{2}}\frac{g_{k}(\eta)}{\sqrt{2k}}\,,

(A.13)

which is of the form (
A.11
) if we write
\eta_{0}=H^{-1}
and account for additional factors of
\eta_{0}
required by dimensional analysis. The substantive difference is that we do not need to extract any factors of
\eta
, so the effective vertex factor in this case is the original vertex factor

V_{i}=i\lambda_{p_{i}}\left(\frac{\eta}{\eta_{0}}\right)^{-(d+1)(1+\varepsilon)}\,.

(A.14)

Comparing this to (
A.12
), we see that the massless field in a power-law cosmology maps to the case of a massive field in de Sitter if we
set
1+\alpha_{i}+\xi_{i}=(d+1)(1+\varepsilon)
.

In the massive case, we had two parameters
\alpha_{i}
(which depends on
d
and
p_{i}
, the number of lines connected to the vertex
i
) and
\xi_{i}
(which depends on the masses of the fields entering the vertex). In the massless case, we instead have the parameters
\varepsilon
,
d
, and
p_{i}
.
It is easy to define a dictionary between those sets of parameters. We first use (
A.10
) to express
\xi\equiv\nu-\frac{1}{2}
in terms
\varepsilon
. We then substitute this into
\alpha_{i}=(d+1)(1+\varepsilon)-1-\xi_{i}
and use the fact that
\xi
is the same for all fields to write
\xi_{i}=p_{i}\xi
. This leads to the following map:

\displaystyle\xi_{i}

\displaystyle=\frac{d-1}{2}(1+\varepsilon)\,p_{i}\,,

(A.15)

\displaystyle\alpha_{i}

\displaystyle=(1+\varepsilon)\left(d+1-\frac{d-1}{2}\,p_{i}\right)-1\,.

(A.16)

With these replacements, the differential equations and the kinematic flow derived in the main text can be applied directly to massless fields in a power-law cosmology.

Appendix B
Combinatorics and Geometry

In Section
3
, we derived first-order differential equations for
the wavefunction coefficients by viewing them as time integrals that sum over the spacetime evolution of the theory.
An interesting complementary approach, summarized in Section
2.3
, is to
cast the integrals of interest as twisted integrals of rational functions in an auxiliary space of energy variables.
In this appendix, we elaborate further on this alternative perspective, which makes contact with geometry and combinatorics.

B.1
Integrals and Combinatorics

The key idea is to use the following integral representation of the Hankel function (see also
[
34
]
)

H_{\nu}^{(2)}(x)=\frac{i}{\sqrt{\pi}}\frac{2^{1+\nu}x^{-\nu}}{\Gamma[\tfrac{1}{2}-\nu]}\int_{1}^{\infty}{\rm d}t\,e^{-ixt}(t^{2}-1)^{-\nu-\frac{1}{2}}\,,

(B.1)

which expresses the Hankel function as an integral over a rational function times an exponential.
13
13

13

Strictly speaking, this representation is only valid for
{\rm Re}\,\nu<1/2
. However, since our ultimate goal is to derive differential equations for
\psi
, we will adopt the philosophy that the parameter
\nu
can be analytically continued directly at the level of the differential equations. Alternatively, we can use the fact that
H_{\nu}^{(2)}(x)=e^{i\pi\nu}H_{-\nu}^{(2)}(x)
to find the equivalent expression

H_{\nu}^{(2)}(x)=\frac{i}{\sqrt{\pi}}\frac{2^{1-\nu}e^{i\nu\pi}x^{\nu}}{\Gamma[\nu+\tfrac{1}{2}]}\int_{1}^{\infty}{\rm d}t\,e^{-ixt}(t^{2}-1)^{\nu-\frac{1}{2}}\,,

(B.2)

which is valid for
{\rm Re}\,\nu>-1/2
.

Using this representation (and its complex conjugate for
H^{(1)}_{\nu}(x)
), we can write the propagators in (
2.16
) as

\displaystyle\hat{K}(k,\eta)

\displaystyle={\cal N}_{k}\,\int_{1}^{\infty}{\rm d}s\,(s^{2}-1)^{-\nu-\frac{1}{2}}\,{\cal K}(k,\eta)\,,

(B.3)

\displaystyle\hat{G}_{\rm F}(k,\eta,\eta^{\prime})

\displaystyle=2k\hskip 1.0pt\lvert{\cal N}_{k}\rvert^{2}\,\int_{1}^{\infty}{\rm d}t_{1}{\rm d}t_{2}\,(t_{1}^{2}-1)^{-\nu-\frac{1}{2}}(t_{2}^{2}-1)^{-\nu-\frac{1}{2}}\,{\cal G}_{\rm F}(k,\eta,\eta^{\prime})\,,

\displaystyle\hat{G}_{\rm D}(k,\eta,\eta^{\prime})

\displaystyle=2k\hskip 1.0pt\lvert{\cal N}_{k}\rvert^{2}\,\int_{1}^{\infty}{\rm d}t_{1}{\rm d}t_{2}\,(t_{1}^{2}-1)^{-\nu-\frac{1}{2}}(t_{2}^{2}-1)^{-\nu-\frac{1}{2}}\,{\cal G}_{\rm D}(k,\eta,\eta^{\prime})\,,

where we have defined the normalization constant

{\cal N}_{k}\equiv\frac{2^{\nu+\frac{1}{2}}}{\Gamma[\tfrac{1}{2}-\nu]}k^{-\xi}\,,

(B.4)

along with the reduced propagators

\displaystyle{\cal K}(k,\eta)

\displaystyle\equiv e^{i(ks)\eta}\,,

(B.5)

\displaystyle{\cal G}_{\rm F}(k,\eta,\eta^{\prime})

\displaystyle\equiv\frac{1}{2k}\left(e^{-ik(t_{1}\eta-t_{2}\eta^{\prime})}\theta(\eta-\eta^{\prime})+e^{-ik(t_{2}\eta^{\prime}-t_{1}\eta)}\theta(\eta^{\prime}-\eta)\right),

\displaystyle{\cal G}_{\rm D}(k,\eta,\eta^{\prime})

\displaystyle\equiv\frac{1}{2k}e^{ik(t_{1}\eta+t_{2}\eta^{\prime})}\,.

The benefit of these various redefinitions is now apparent: the reduced propagators take exactly the same form as those of a scalar field in flat space. The novel feature is that each internal line has two energy variables
kt_{1}
and
kt_{2}
, which are integrated over.

The reason for introducing the integral representation of the Hankel function is that the integrals over time simplify.
Recall that each vertex has a factor

V_{i}=i\lambda_{i}(-\eta_{i})^{-(1+\gamma_{i})}=-\lambda_{i}\,\frac{i^{\gamma_{i}}}{\Gamma[1+\gamma_{i}]}\int_{0}^{\infty}{\rm d}x\,x^{\gamma_{i}}e^{ix\eta_{i}}\,,

(B.6)

where
\gamma_{i}\equiv\alpha_{i}+\xi_{i}
, with
\alpha_{i}
and
\xi_{i}
defined in (
2.18
). In the second equality of (
B.6
), we have expressed the polynomial factor in (conformal) time as an energy integral
[
5
]
.
14
14

14

Note that in some cases

\alpha_{i}
will be positive. In these cases, the integer part of this combination should be written as derivatives with respect to vertex energies, with the remainder parametrized as an energy integral.

This will allow us to perform all the time integrals and write the wavefunction as an integral of a rational integrand.
In practice, we will be interested in the limit
\eta_{*}\to 0
, where the constants appearing in (
2.15
) simplify for real values of
\nu
. In particular, we then have
C_{k}^{({\rm D})}=C_{k}^{({\rm F})}
. This simplification makes it easy to recombine these pieces at the level of the integrand. In cases involving principal series fields, the relative factor between the Feynman and disconnected propagators is more complicated, and we will denote it abstractly by
A
, keeping in mind that
A=1
for real
\nu
.

Universal integrand

The wavefunction coefficient
\psi

for arbitrary internal and external states becomes a (twisted) integral over the parameters
s,t,x
of a
universal integrand
,
\uppsi
. This universal integrand can be obtained via the usual Feynman rules with the building blocks (
B.5
) and (
B.6
). The physical states and interactions of interest then dictate how we twist this integrand and integrate it.

Let us illustrate this with the example of a two-site massive exchange:

\displaystyle\uppsi^{(2)}

}

(B.7)

\displaystyle=-\int{\rm d}\eta_{1}{\rm d}\eta_{2}\,e^{iX_{1}\eta_{1}}e^{iX_{2}\eta_{2}}\Big[{\cal G}_{\rm F}(\eta_{1},\eta_{2})-A\,{\cal G}_{\rm D}(\eta_{1},\eta_{2})\Big]\,,

where we have labeled the graph by the energies
X_{a}
(
a=1,2
) of each external vertex, its internal vertex energy
Y
, and the variables
t_{L,R}
associated to the internal line. Since the integrand does not depend on the number of external lines emanating from a vertex, it makes sense to truncate the external lines as we have done.
We have also marked the internal line with a white circle to note the fact that the internal energy can change in the exchange (which will eventually be integrated over).
Performing the time integrals, we obtain

\uppsi^{(2)}=\uppsi^{(2)}_{\rm F}-A\,\uppsi^{(2)}_{\rm D}\,,

(B.8)

where the time-ordered and disconnected pieces are

\displaystyle\uppsi^{(2)}_{\rm F}

\displaystyle\equiv\frac{1}{2Y}\bigg[\frac{1}{X_{1}+X_{2}+(t_{L}-t_{R})Y}\frac{1}{X_{1}+t_{L}Y}+\frac{1}{X_{1}+X_{2}+(t_{R}-t_{L})Y}\frac{1}{X_{2}+t_{R}Y}\bigg]\,,

(B.9)

\displaystyle\uppsi^{(2)}_{\rm D}

\displaystyle\equiv\frac{1}{2Y}\,\frac{1}{X_{1}+t_{L}Y}\frac{1}{X_{2}+t_{R}Y}\,.

How we integrate this universal integrand depends on the situation we are interested in.
In all cases of interest, we integrate over the internal variables
t_{b}
(
b=L,R
), weighted by the twist factors
(t_{b}^{2}-1)^{-\nu-\frac{1}{2}}
, and shift the external variables
X_{a}\mapsto X_{a}+x_{a}
and then integrate over
x_{a}
with the appropriate twist.
If in addition the external lines are themselves massive, we write the shift of the external energies as
x_{a}+s_{1}+\cdots+s_{n}
, and then also integrate over the
s
variables (again with the appropriate twist). As an example, the four-point function of conformally coupled scalar fields exchanging a field of general mass in four-dimensional de Sitter space is given by the following integral (up to an overall
Y
-dependent normalization factor)

\psi^{(2)}\sim\int\bigg(\prod_{a=1,2}{\rm d}x_{a}\,x_{a}^{\xi}\prod_{b=L,R}{\rm d}t_{b}\,(t_{b}^{2}-1)^{-\nu-\frac{1}{2}}\bigg)\,\uppsi(X_{a}+x_{a},t_{b}Y)\,,

(B.10)

where the integrand is a rational function with linear factors. The integrand therefore naturally has an associated hyperplane arrangement and the machinery of twisted cohomology can be applied. We will explore some aspects of this in Section
B.2
.

It is straightforward to cast the wavefunction involving arbitrary states as a similar twisted integral by using the propagators in (
B.5
). However, performing the time integrals to obtain a rational integrand quickly becomes fairly tedious, so it is useful to organize the calculation into an (equivalent) combinatorial mnemonic.

Combinatorics

The time integrals that compute the universal massive integrand have a nice combinatorial structure that we can exploit to
give a direct algorithm for its construction.

Graphs and maximal tubings:
The integrand is a rational function, and so it can naturally be related to tubings of a (labeled) graph.
For the massive integrands, the natural graph is the underlying Feynman diagram that we use to compute
\uppsi
. It is convenient to mark the internal lines of the graph with a white circle as in (
B.7
) to keep track of the fact that the internal energy flowing through the graph is different on the two sides of the marking.
In addition, it will be convenient to distinguish between time-ordered internal lines (which we denote by solid lines) and disconnected internal lines (which we denote by dotted lines).

With this understanding, the terms in the time-integral representation of
\uppsi
are in one-to-one correspondence with the maximal tubings of these graphs.
15
15

15

A
tube

[
20
,
27
]
is a proper non-empty subset of a graph, so that the nodes contained in the tube yield a connected subgraph. Tubes are
compatible
in the sense of
[
20
,
27
]
if they do not intersect and are not adjacent. A
tubing
is a collection of pairwise compatible tubes. For clarity, we will call such a tubing a
math tubing
(since it relies on the notion of compatibility common in the mathematics literature) in order to distinguish it from a slightly different notion of tubing which will appear in Section
4
.
Since a tubing is a proper subset, it can contain at most
n-1
tubes for a
n
-vertex graph. Such a tubing with
n-1
tubes is a
maximal tubing
. It is important to specify that the white dots on internal lines are
not
vertices, and so by convention we always leave them outside tubes when the tube does not fully enclose an internal line.

This correspondence between tubings and the time-integral representation of the wavefunction is a consequence of the fact that a maximal tubing induces an orientation on the graph, obtained by drawing arrows that point away from each tube, starting from the smallest tube and working outwards.

(B.12)

We see that both tubings lead to the same pattern of arrows. This is expected from the time integral. For this time ordering, there are two integration regions, depending on whether the leftmost or rightmost vertex is the latest, and so it is satisfying that the combinatorial construction naturally splits up these two contributions.

Rational function:
We now describe the algorithm to produce
\uppsi
, before illustrating it with some simple examples.
Starting from the Feynman graph (with truncated external lines), we consider all maximal tubings. We then associate a linear factor to each tube in a given maximal tubing.
Specifically, to each tube we assign the sum of energies of all (black) vertices enclosed along with the sum of energies carried by lines piercing the tube. For tubes that enclose an internal white dot, we also add
(t_{L}-t_{R})Y
or
(t_{R}-t_{L})Y
, depending on the direction that the arrow is pointing (the direction the arrow points away from gets the
+
sign). We divide by each of these linear factors. For example, the tubing in (
B.12
) leads to

}=\frac{1}{{\color[rgb]{0.582,0,0.8281}X_{2}+X_{3}+t^{R}_{12}Y_{12}+(t_{23}^{L}-t_{23}^{R})Y_{23}}}\frac{1}{{\color[rgb]{0.8398,0.1523,0.1563}X_{2}+t_{12}^{R}Y_{12}+t_{23}^{L}Y_{23}}}\,.

(B.13)

To obtain the wavefunction, we also associate a “universal tube” to each
maximal tubing that encloses the entire graph, and assign it a linear factor following the same rules.
Each maximal tubing gives a contribution to
\uppsi
that is
1
divided by the product of these linear factors, along with a factor of
1/(2Y_{i})
for each internal line. We sum up all the contributions for the fully connected graph, and then proceed to dash each of the internal lines in all possible ways, and repeat the procedure with each of these disconnected graphs. The wavefunction integrand
\uppsi
is the sum of all of these pieces with weight
(-A)
for each disconnected internal line.

An example:

Let us illustrate the procedure for the case of the single massive exchange.
The underlying Feynman graph is the same as in (
B.7
). We first consider the connected graph, which has two maximal tubings:

\displaystyle=\frac{1}{2Y}\,\frac{1}{{\color[rgb]{0.1211,0.4648,0.707}X_{1}+X_{2}+(t_{L}-t_{R})Y}}\frac{1}{{\color[rgb]{0.8398,0.1523,0.1563}X_{1}+t_{L}Y}}\,,

(B.14)

\displaystyle=\frac{1}{2Y}\,\frac{1}{{\color[rgb]{0.1211,0.4648,0.707}X_{1}+X_{2}+(t_{R}-t_{L})Y}}\frac{1}{{\color[rgb]{0.8398,0.1523,0.1563}X_{2}+t_{R}Y}}\,,

(B.15)

where we have written the corresponding rational functions. In addition, there is a single disconnected graph with a dashed internal line:

\displaystyle=\ \,\frac{1}{4Y_{12}Y_{23}}\frac{1}{{\color[rgb]{0.1211,0.4648,0.707}X_{1}+t_{12}^{L}Y_{12}}}\frac{1}{{\color[rgb]{0.8398,0.1523,0.1563}X_{2}+t_{12}^{R}Y_{12}+t_{23}^{L}Y_{23}}}\hskip 79.6678pt\phantom{x}

(B.18)

\displaystyle\times\frac{1}{{\color[rgb]{0.1211,0.4648,0.707}X_{2}+X_{3}+t_{12}^{R}Y_{12}+(t_{23}^{L}-t_{23}^{R})Y_{23}}}\,.

Finally, there is one fully disconnected contribution, which has a single maximal tubing (with each vertex circled). As before, adding up all these contributions (weighted by
(-A)
for each disconnected line) reproduces the universal integrand obtained by integrating the Feynman rules.

This procedure can be given a formal proof along the lines of
[
5
]
, which computes bulk time integrals directly by successively collapsing internal lines in a way compatible with the graph orientation and combining the energies. The end result matches the output of this combinatorial exercise.
An interesting feature of this massive case is that the time-integral representation does not produce any spurious singularities (in contrast to the conformally coupled case).

B.2
Massive Geometries

One of the nice features of the above representation is that it casts the integrals of interest in a (twisted) Euler form. Since the factors appearing in the integrand are linear, the integrals are naturally associated to hyperplane arrangements
[
57
,
53
,
49
]
. As such, these integrals can be given a geometric interpretation, and the tools of positive geometry and twisted cohomology can be systematically employed. Most basically, this makes it clear that the massive wavefunction is part of a finite-dimensional vector space of integrals, and therefore is part of a first-order system of differential equations.

Figure 1
:
Visualization of the hyperplane arrangement defined by the singularities of the massive two-site integral in the
x_{1}
-
x_{2}
plane.

Hyperplane arrangements

Describing the full features of the geometry underlying the universal massive integrand would take us too far afield from the main line of development. We take up this study in future work. Here, we content ourselves with describing the simplest nontrivial example of the two-site exchange graph.
Combining the terms appearing in (
B.8
), the function
\uppsi^{(2)}
can be written as
16
16

16

It is worth noting that for real
\nu
, the two obviously special values of
A
have natural interpretations. The value
A=1
corresponds to the wavefunction, while
A=-1
gives the corresponding in-in correlator
[
14
,
32
,
36
]
. In both cases there is a simplification of the numerator.

\uppsi^{(2)}=\frac{1}{2Y}\frac{(1-A)(X_{1}+X_{2})^{2}+2(t_{L}X_{1}+t_{R}X_{2})Y+(1+A)(t_{L}-t_{R})^{2}Y^{2}}{(X_{1}+t_{L}Y)(X_{2}+t_{R}Y)(X_{1}+X_{2}+(t_{L}-t_{R})Y)(X_{1}+X_{2}+(t_{R}-t_{L})Y)}\,.

(B.19)

Writing all terms under a single denominator makes all singularities of the object manifest. The singularities are given by the vanishing loci of the following five lines

\displaystyle\color[rgb]{0.8398,0.1523,0.1563}{L_{1}}

\displaystyle\color[rgb]{0.8398,0.1523,0.1563}{\displaystyle\equiv X_{1}+X_{2}+x_{1}+x_{2}+(t_{R}-t_{L})Y}\,,

(B.20)

\displaystyle\color[rgb]{0.582,0,0.8281}{L_{2}}

\displaystyle\color[rgb]{0.582,0,0.8281}{\displaystyle\equiv X_{2}+x_{2}+t_{R}\hskip 1.0ptY}\,,

\displaystyle\color[rgb]{1,0.4961,0.0547}{L_{3}}

\displaystyle\color[rgb]{1,0.4961,0.0547}{\displaystyle\equiv X_{1}+X_{2}+x_{1}+x_{2}+(t_{L}-t_{R})Y}\,,

\displaystyle\color[rgb]{0.1719,0.6289,0.1719}{L_{4}}

\displaystyle\color[rgb]{0.1719,0.6289,0.1719}{\displaystyle\equiv X_{1}+x_{1}+t_{L}\hskip 1.0ptY}\,,

\displaystyle L_{5}

\displaystyle=Y\,,

which defines a hyperplane arrangement in the (projective) space of integration variables
x_{1,2}
and
t_{L,R}
. To visualize this arrangement, it is convenient to project either onto the two-dimensional spaces of
x
or
t
-variables. In the
x
-space, the singular lines of (
B.19
) correspond to the geometric picture shown in Fig.
1
.
This allows us to view the integrand (
B.19
) as the canonical form of a geometric region in the space of
x
-variables. The simplest such association can be made by defining the dlog-form

[L_{1}\cdots L_{n}]\equiv{\rm d}\log L_{1}\wedge\cdots\wedge{\rm d}\log L_{n}\,,

(B.21)

so that the two-site integrand corresponds to the following sum of canonical forms associated to unbounded regions

\uppsi^{(2)}\,{\rm d}x_{1}\wedge{\rm d}x_{2}=[L_{3}L_{4}]-[L_{1}L_{2}]+A\hskip 1.0pt[L_{2}L_{4}]\,.

(B.22)

Alternatively, we can view (
B.19
) as the canonical form of a non-convex weighted geometry, corresponding to the gray-shaded region in Fig.
1

[
14
]
.

Integral basis

It is interesting to investigate the integral basis used in the main text through this geometric lens (see Section
2.3
). To do this, it is useful to visualize the hyperplane arrangement associated to (
B.19
) in the
t
-space; see Fig.
2
.

Figure 2
:
Visualization of the hyperplane arrangement defined by the singular lines of the massive two-site integral in the
t_{L}
-
t_{R}
plane. Note that in addition to the singularities defined by the rational integrand, the twist factors define two pairs of singular lines
t_{L}\pm 1
and
t_{R}\pm 1
.

Comparing this arrangement with the analogous one in
x
-space (Fig.
1
), a notable difference is that the twist factors involving
t_{L,R}
correspond to two pairs of singular lines
t_{L}\pm 1
and
t_{R}\pm 1
. In (
B.10
), both of these singularities are twisted with the same parameter. It is natural to allow these two lines to be twisted by different amounts and consider the integrals

\psi^{({\color[rgb]{0.8398,0.1523,0.1563}{\pm}}{\color[rgb]{0.1211,0.4648,0.707}{\pm}})}\equiv\int\bigg(\prod_{a=1,2}{\rm d}x_{a}\,x_{a}^{\xi}\prod_{b=L,R}{\rm d}t_{b}\,(t_{b}^{2}-1)^{-\nu-\frac{1}{2}}\bigg)\,(1\,{\color[rgb]{0.8398,0.1523,0.1563}{\mp}}\,t_{L})(1\,{\color[rgb]{0.1211,0.4648,0.707}{\pm}}\,t_{R})\,\uppsi^{(2)}(X_{a}+x_{a},t_{b}Y)\,,

(B.23)

where the twists of the
(1\,\pm\,t_{L,R})
singularities are shifted by one unit.
One recovers the wavefunction by summing over all these basis elements as
\psi=\psi^{(++)}+\psi^{(--)}+\psi^{(+-)}+\psi^{(-+)}
.

Appendix C
One-Loop Bubble

The explicit examples in the main text all involved tree-level graphs, but it is worth emphasizing that the kinematic flow algorithm presented in Section
4
also applies to
loop integrands
(i.e. to loop-level wavefunctions before integrating over the three-momentum running in the loop, but after integrating over time.)
In fact, one nice feature of the massive case—as compared to the conformally coupled case—is that it is more uniform. The rules are precisely the same at both tree and loop level.
In the conformal case,
many of the basis functions identically vanish, and so
one must modify the flow rules to accommodate this
[
9
,
40
]
. In contrast, the massive case is fully generic, so all graphs follow the same rules.

In this appendix, we will illustrate the application of the procedure at loop level through the simplest example of the
one-loop bubble (with conformally coupled external legs):

X_{1}
X_{2}
Y_{u}
Y_{d}

(C.1)

Here, the “up” (
u
) and “down” (
d
) loop propagators have energies
Y_{u}
and
Y_{d}
and mass parameters
\nu_{u}=\frac{1}{2}+\xi_{u}
and
\nu_{d}=\frac{1}{2}+\xi_{d}
, respectively.

C.1
Letters and Functions

We begin by presenting the letters and basis functions for the one-loop bubble (
C.1
). As in the previous examples, we truncate the (conformally coupled) external lines and mark the internal lines. The letters and functions then correspond to tubings of this marked graph, as in Section
4.1
.

Letters

The following shows the letters appearing in the differential equations for the one-loop bubble:

\penalty\ =\penalty\ {\rm d}\log(X_{1}+Y_{u}+Y_{d})\,,

\penalty\ =\penalty\ {\rm d}\log(X_{2}+Y_{u}+Y_{d})\,,

\penalty\ =\penalty\ {\rm d}\log(X_{1}+Y_{u}-Y_{d})\,,

\penalty\ =\penalty\ {\rm d}\log(X_{2}+Y_{u}-Y_{d})\,,

\penalty\ =\penalty\ {\rm d}\log(X_{1}-Y_{u}+Y_{d})\,,

\penalty\ =\penalty\ {\rm d}\log(X_{2}-Y_{u}+Y_{d})\,,

\penalty\ =\penalty\ {\rm d}\log(X_{1}-Y_{u}-Y_{d})\,,

\penalty\ =\penalty\ {\rm d}\log(X_{2}-Y_{u}-Y_{d})\,,

\penalty\ =\penalty\ {\rm d}\log(X_{1}+X_{2}+2Y_{u})\,,

\penalty\ =\penalty\ {\rm d}\log(X_{1}+X_{2}+2Y_{d})\,,

\penalty\ =\penalty\ {\rm d}\log(Y_{u})\,,

\penalty\ =\penalty\ {\rm d}\log(Y_{d})\,.

(C.2)

Note that there are five equivalent representations of the total energy singularity:

\begin{tabular}[]{ccccc}\includegraphics[valign]{Figures/Tubings/Bubble_Letters/DlogX1+X2.pdf}&\includegraphics[valign]{Figures/Tubings/Bubble_Letters/Zero1.pdf}&\includegraphics[valign]{Figures/Tubings/Bubble_Letters/Zero2.pdf}&\includegraphics[valign]{Figures/Tubings/Bubble_Letters/Zero3.pdf}&\includegraphics[valign]{Figures/Tubings/Bubble_Letters/Zero4.pdf}\end{tabular}={\rm d}\log(X_{1}+X_{2})\,.

(C.3)

We will see how each of these arises in the differential equations satisfied by the bubble.

Functions

As in the main text, we restrict attention to fully connected diagrams. The functions associated with the one-loop bubble are then obtained by the same procedure as in Section
4.1
.
It is straightforward to write down the tubing representation of each of these functions using the same rule as before.

We first consider tubings where each tube only contains one vertex.
We label these functions by
\psi^{(\pm\pm)}_{(\pm\pm)}
, where we
assign a minus sign when a tube encircles the corresponding cross and plus sign when it does not:

\psi^{(++)}_{(++)}

\psi^{(-+)}_{(++)}

\psi^{(+-)}_{(++)}

\psi^{(+-)}_{(-+)}

\psi^{(+-)}_{(+-)}

\psi^{(++)}_{(-+)}

\psi^{(++)}_{(+-)}

\psi^{(-+)}_{(+-)}

\psi^{(-+)}_{(-+)}

\psi^{(--)}_{(--)}

\psi^{(+-)}_{(--)}

\psi^{(-+)}_{(--)}

\psi^{(--)}_{(++)}

\psi^{(--)}_{(+-)}

\psi^{(--)}_{(-+)}

\psi^{(++)}_{(--)}

(C.4)

Similar to what happens at tree level, the (connected) wavefunction coefficient
\psi
is obtained by adding up these
16
functions.
There are 12 basis functions corresponding to the tubings with exposed crosses and overlapping tubes. As we will show in Section
C.3
, these vanish in the conformal limit.

Additional functions appear when differentiating
\psi^{(\pm\pm)}_{(\pm\pm)}
. From the time-integral perspective, they correspond to collapsing internal propagators. Here, they are represented by tubes that contain two vertices:

(C.5)

As we will show below, the rightmost tubing doesn’t actually appear in the kinematic flow equations. Of the remaining 8 tubings, only 6 are actually independent functions.

C.2
Massive Kinematic Flow

In Section
4.2
, we stated the three rules of the kinematic flow and illustrated them in selected tree-level examples. The same rules, without any modifications, apply to the differential equations for loop integrands. It is instructive to see this explicitly for the case of the one-loop bubble.

For concreteness, let us consider the function
\psi^{(-+)}_{(-+)}
. It satisfies the differential equation

(C.8)

The coefficient is the difference of the two letters corresponding to the two tubes involved in the merger.

3.

Mixing
: Both tubes of the parent function are pierced by the massive propagators and therefore can
grow
and
shrink
to produce new source functions. There are four ways in which this can happen, so we get

(C.10)

The terms on the right-hand side arise from activation and mixing. Note that there is no contribution from merger, despite the fact that the two sides of the tube on the left-hand side are adjacent to each other. A tube cannot merge with itself; instead we require two different tubes that are adjacent in order for merger to occur.
17
17

17

Alternatively, one could allow the self-merger of a tube, but the coefficient of the resulting source in the differential equation would be the difference of the same letter and itself, giving zero.
A consequence of this is that the rightmost tubing in (
C.5
) will never appear in the kinematic flow.

One can repeat this for all basis functions. In addition,
starting from the time-integral representation, it is straightforward to verify that this
kinematic flow procedure gives the correct differential equations for all basis functions of the one-loop bubble.

C.3
Conformal Limit

It is interesting to explore the conformally coupled limit of this system of differential equations, corresponding to
\xi_{u},\xi_{d}\to 0
. In this limit, there is a drastic reduction in the size of the function basis. We can understand this from the
explicit expressions for the basis functions in (
C.4
):

\displaystyle\psi^{({\color[rgb]{0.8398,0.1523,0.1563}{\pm}}{\color[rgb]{0.1211,0.4648,0.707}{\pm}})}_{({\color[rgb]{0.8398,0.1523,0.1563}{\pm}}{\color[rgb]{0.1211,0.4648,0.707}{\pm}})}=\int\frac{{\rm d}\eta_{1}\,e^{iX_{1}\eta_{1}}}{(-\eta_{1})^{1+\alpha_{1}+\xi_{u}+\xi_{d}}}\frac{{\rm d}\eta_{2}\,e^{iX_{2}\eta_{2}}}{(-\eta_{2})^{1+\alpha_{2}+\xi_{u}+\xi_{d}}}\,\bigg[\Big(\bar{h}_{Y_{u}}^{{\color[rgb]{0.8398,0.1523,0.1563}{\pm}}}(\eta_{1})\bar{h}_{Y_{d}}^{{\color[rgb]{0.8398,0.1523,0.1563}{\pm}}}(\eta_{1})h_{Y_{u}}^{{\color[rgb]{0.1211,0.4648,0.707}{\pm}}}(\eta_{2})h_{Y_{d}}^{{\color[rgb]{0.1211,0.4648,0.707}{\pm}}}(\eta_{2})\Big)

\displaystyle\theta_{12}

(C.11)

\displaystyle+\Big(h_{Y_{u}}^{{\color[rgb]{0.8398,0.1523,0.1563}{\pm}}}(\eta_{1})h_{Y_{d}}^{{\color[rgb]{0.8398,0.1523,0.1563}{\pm}}}(\eta_{1})\bar{h}_{Y_{u}}^{{\color[rgb]{0.1211,0.4648,0.707}{\pm}}}(\eta_{2})\bar{h}_{Y_{d}}^{{\color[rgb]{0.1211,0.4648,0.707}{\pm}}}(\eta_{2})\Big)

\displaystyle\theta_{21}\bigg]\,.

Recall that in the conformally coupled limit,
h_{k}^{-}=\bar{h}_{k}^{+}=0
. This means that the majority of the basis functions in (
C.4
) vanish. The only functions that survive the limit are
\psi^{(-+)}_{(-+)}
and
\psi^{(+-)}_{(+-)}
.
18
18

18

Mechanically, the vanishing of these functions can be traced to two different mechanisms. The first is that the propagator associated to an internal line identically vanishes. This happens for the
++
or
--
assignments, so any
\psi
with one of these assignments in either a superscript or a subscript vanishes. This is responsible for the vanishing of 12 of the functions in (
C.4
). The remaining two functions vanish because the emergent time ordering of the propagators (discussed in Section
4.1
) is incompatible.
The tubings corresponding to these functions can naturally be given an orientation that agrees with the time ordering of the time integral. Explicitly, we have

. It is important to emphasize that the massive integrals do not have a definite time ordering because they have a mixture of theta functions. However, in the conformal limit, one of the theta function terms vanishes, so the propagators in the conformally coupled limit have a definite time order.

The simplification of the collapsed terms is even more pronounced. As enumerated in (
C.5
), there are 9 possible tubings involving collapsed terms. However, as discussed above, only 8 of these appear in the kinematic flow equations, of which 6 are independent.

\displaystyle=\frac{1}{2}\int{\rm d}\eta\,\zeta_{d}\,\bigg(h^{+}_{Y_{d}}(\eta)\bar{h}^{-}_{Y_{d}}(\eta)+h^{-}_{Y_{d}}(\eta)\bar{h}^{+}_{Y_{d}}(\eta)\bigg)\,,

where we have defined

\zeta_{a}\equiv\frac{e^{i(X_{1}+X_{2})\eta}}{(-\eta)^{1+\alpha_{1}+\alpha_{2}+2\xi_{a}}}\,,\quad{\rm for}\quad a=u,d\,.

(C.14)

Here, we see explicitly which functions coincide in the massive case.
(Note that the equality of the pair of tubings in the last two lines of (
C.13
) can also be verified from the kinematic flow, since they satisfy identical differential equations.)
In the conformal limit, we have
h_{k}^{-}=\bar{h}_{k}^{+}=0
, along with
h_{k}^{+}=e^{ik\eta}
and
\bar{h}_{k}^{-}=e^{-ik\eta}
. It is easy to see that this makes the first four functions in (
C.13
) vanish, while the last four functions become identical and equal to one half of the function associated with the fully encircled tubing:

(C.15)

It makes sense to denote all of these equivalent functions by the fully circled tubing. In this case, the merger step of the kinematic flow in (
C.8
) can also be reinterpreted as a double merging that results in a collapsed function with fully encircled tubing
[
9
]
.

The same procedure can readily be applied to more complex processes involving more internal propagators or more loops.
The main takeaway is twofold: First, the massive kinematic flow behaves the same way for loop integrands as it does at tree level. In fact, this may be viewed as an advantage of this generalization. Second, in the conformally coupled limit, there are substantial simplifications due to the fact that many of the functions vanish. The massive flow rules then reduce to those of
[
9
,
40
,
8
]
, suitably interpreted.
